other_moves.move: Staged fps business case for the 2050 round (authority-to-offer work)
other_moves.detail:
Solo by default. Pope's IP test finds that Embraer brings no airframe IP or capacity we lack: its partnership is with CFM, and via Embraer sits $4.04-4.23B below the Solo 10-year.

The base case is the 10-year ramp. It beats the 7-year by 0.88-1.14 in every column, has the higher worst column, and holds stress net debt at $0.

Renton only with Pope's five-step MAX bridge plan:
1. No conversion before the fps type certificate.
2. Each Renton line comes down only after the fps line has held rate for 2-3 stable KPI months.
3. One Renton MAX line stays warm until the fps reaches about 50 a month.
4. The LEAP-1B allocation follows the actual wind-down.
5. The Everett North Line carries the tail at up to 15 a month.

Code 7 (CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture), with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition. Design the production system with the airplane and prove it at rate before authority to offer. Type certificate before rate; no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].

The case must show:
- the item value in S1, S2 and S3 against the Board's two lines;
- Malave's slip leg as the baseline, with the clean-sheet prior (+3 years) and a cost-overrun sensitivity (does the item survive a 2% overrun?) priced in full, once;
- the cost of waiting under the public lead-edge rule.

Decide the fps and the 787 Re-engine together, as one pair, under H4: both held to 2050 gives 2 years with a 10-year fps and 5 with a 7-year. If the 2050 case does not clear, we say so and do not force it.

other_moves.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle (updated to the record)
other_moves.detail: We continue to invite the narrowbody engine makers to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. With GTF2 and UltraFan NB now folded into the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, our plan at launch is a choice of two engine sources: CFM and the Joint Venture (code 7). Selection is on value among engines actually launched, with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition. No fps date and no launch commitment.

other_moves.move: 737 MAX back to full output at 57 a month, KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA
other_moves.detail: As demand comes back, the 737 returns to its 57-a-month ceiling. This is not a Rate Increase. Each step is taken one at a time, only after stable KPIs and agreement with the FAA, and only when supplier and engine output for the next step is proven. No step dates are published.

other_moves.move: MAX climb-back ladder and supplier gates (internal plan)
Keep the trained workforce and fragile suppliers funded through the climb
other_moves.detail: Bring back the trained people kept through the 2038-44 dip, and train for the ladder first. Then form a protected fps production-system team that does not draw on the line. Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources [BX-1243, B-2330]. The suppliers that carry 52 and 57 are the ones a 2050 fps would load next.

other_moves.move: 787 Re-engine: study only, no launch
other_moves.detail:
Engine basis: the GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033. Recorded candidly: the item has shrunk by ten years of discounting (2.01 in 2035 to 0.74 now), and a 2050 launch is about +0.45, below ε at any probability of an A350 Re-engine. This hold very probably closes it on this board.

Re-test it in 2050 only if H3's second half is still open (no A350 Re-engine on the record), and only as one pair with any fps under H4. No programme spend is committed.

other_moves.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
other_moves.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

other_moves.move: No shareholder-return signal
other_moves.detail: Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress. Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board. Keep headroom for a staged fps ($60.32B on the 10-year ramp, about $8.44B in its peak year, 92% of stress free cash flow). Nothing is said publicly.

boeing.public_statement:
Five years ago I said I thought we'd turned the ship. We have, and the job now is to keep it steady. The balance sheet is repaired and it's staying repaired. The 777X and the 737 MAX family are delivering, and the 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class.

On the 737, we're bringing the line back to full output, 57 a month, as demand comes back. We'll take that one step at a time. Each step comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity, and when we and the FAA agree the line is ready. We'll make sure our suppliers and our engine supply are there before each step. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early.

On a new airplane: we're not launching one this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. I'll tell you plainly what's changed. The market case is better than it was. It isn't there yet. We will do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing are all ready. Technology is ready, and Boeing is ready. The market is getting there, but it hasn't got there. The work goes on in stages. We're designing the production system together with the airplane, so that when we go, we go on a conservative plan with headroom in it, with no fixed-price development risk, and we build it at rate the right way.

On engines, we've updated our requirement. Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are now one Joint Venture, so our plan is to give customers a choice of two engine sources at launch, CFM and the Joint Venture, with durability proven before entry into service.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year. We'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

Our dates are set by our own readiness. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every lever. fps hold, fps_site new_site, fps_engine_code null, re787 hold, rate_737 hold.
- Submitted row: -1.01 / -1.34 / -1.01 (S1 / S2 / S3).
- Nothing differs from the default, so there is no Board item.

TEAM RULE
- Malave's buffer veto binds on all four via-Embraer rows (S3 -4.68 to -5.13, 1.67-2.12 past the -3.01 line). None is chosen.
- The KPI doctrine has no object: rate_737 is hold only, and no problem is live.
- Pope flagged H4 on the 7-year fps + Re-engine (5 years) and on a 10-year fps now with a 2050 Re-engine (5 years). Neither is chosen.
- No flag needs a strike, and there are no overrides.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. KPIs stable? Yes. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem [BX-1271]. The FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
2. Market, technology and Boeing all ready [BX-1296, BX-1305]?
   - Technology: yes. CFM is always ready, and the Joint Venture has been ready since 2036.
   - Balance sheet: yes. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 in base and stress, the 777X turned in 2029 [BX-0547], and Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' gate passes for any 10-year row.
   - Market: turning, not turned. Demand above both makers' slots from 2047 moved the fps item from -1.20 to +0.07, about $0.51B of it real. That is still a tie, not a case [BX-1300].
3. What if certification takes longer? S3 equals S1 on every row, so the printed slip leg prices nothing. Malave priced the slip instead:
   - fps: on the clean-sheet prior of +3 years, any slip cost above about $1.0B (1.7% of the bill) turns the 10-year at Renton negative. The 777X reset alone was $4.9B [BX-0550].
   - Pope: a 2.1% overrun erases it on its own.
   - Re-engine: the derivative prior takes it to +0.61.
   So I plan for the reset, once [BX-1318, BX-1319], and the fps edge does not survive it.
4. Doing less, better [BX-1239]? Every plan within ε of Do Nothing in S1 (+0.74, +0.56, +0.41, +0.07, -0.08, ...) loses to doing less. Do Nothing is also the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]: it has nothing to slip.

DEBT FIRST (the grid already nets the penalty; not subtracted again)
- No plan beats Do Nothing by more than ε in S1.
- Undiscounted penalties, for scale only: 10-year $19.1B against a $0.07B netted edge; Re-engine $0.6B.

TIE-BREAK ON WORST COLUMN
Malave reports plainly that on the printed grid the 10-year at Renton has the higher worst column (S2 -1.27 against -1.34). That $0.07B edge equals the item value at a nominal 2055 date and a nominal bill, and goes with any slip cost above about $1.0B. My first tie-break is doing less, and his slip-priced test also picks Do Nothing.

PER-ROW RESULTS (item values S1 / S2 / S3 against the default)
- Re-engine alone: +0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74.
  - Best in S1, but inside ε and below the Board's +$1B line, whatever the probability p of an A350 Re-engine (0.74 - 1.55p).
  - Its worst column, -2.15, is 0.81 below Do Nothing's.
  - Board hold, logged separately.
- 10-year at Renton: +0.07 in every column; at new sites -0.08.
  - Fails my debt-first ε and the Board's +$1B line by $0.93B.
  - Passes buffer (S3 -0.94, headroom +2.07), Downside, H4 and net debt $0 in base and stress.
- 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: +0.56 / -0.99 / +0.56 against Do Nothing.
  - Its Re-engine item falls to -1.06 in S2, which fails the Board's Downside line.
  - H4 sits at its 2-year limit with no slack, and reaches 4 years on a 2-year derivative slip.
- 7-year rows: closed. They sit 0.88-1.14 below the 10-year. Stress net debt fails at new sites ($0.7B) and with the Re-engine ($2.0-3.1B). With the Re-engine they breach H4 at 5 years, and their strain window lands on the MAX climb (Pope).
- Via Embraer: closed by Malave's binding veto. It is $4.04-4.23B below Solo, carries a $52.5B undiscounted penalty, fails stress ($1.5-6.3B) and fails Pope's IP test.

RED LINES AND HARD RULES
- H1 and H3's first half: lifted in my 2030 ruling, not re-made.
- H3's second half: confirmed open. No A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- H4, H5, H6 and H8: respected. Soft total $0.07B.
- Mine: no production-certification concurrency, no fixed-price development, and no step in the MAX climb without stable KPIs.

COST OF WAITING (information, not a reason)
- On the grid, about $0.03B: a 2050 launch is worth at most about +0.04.
- In share under the lead-edge rule, unscored and after 2050: the long-run split falls from 32% (10-year now, EIS 2055) or 35% (7-year now, EIS 2052) to 27% (10-year, EIS 2060) or 30% (7-year, EIS 2057).
- I say it honestly: on this board's demand path the fps may never clear the Board's line, and this hold very probably closes the 787 Re-engine.
- Building a new future is on my list [BX-1245]; chasing share is not, and Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313].

RECORD VS DOCTRINE
- My record drove: the hold (doing less [BX-1239]; three streams [BX-1296]; slip planning [BX-1319]); the KPI-gated, FAA-agreed climb [BX-1259, BX-1322]; and keeping suppliers funded [BX-1243].
- Doctrine drove: code 7 in the engine requirement (Low confidence: I have no record on engine choice); the 10-year/Renton base for 2050; logging the Re-engine as a Board hold; and the A350 probability read, which is Malave's and doctrine.

BIASES: stability over share, under-disclosure (no dates, ladder kept internal), and cash for readiness are all displayed at no grid cost.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Jay's memo was weighed heavily on estimates, the buffer and the slip, as my independent check [BX-1316]. It is a thin seat, though: his record is one call (Low), so beyond the buffer test his views are inference or doctrine, and I treated them as advice.

Taken as binding:
- The buffer veto on every via-Embraer row (S3 -4.68 to -5.13). Accepted; none is chosen.

Taken as decisive input:
- The slip pricing. On the +3-year clean-sheet prior, a slip cost above about $1.0B turns the 10-year at Renton negative, which removes its $0.07B edge in S2.
- The 'Fundable when the 777X turns' pass, and the net-debt line ($0 in base and stress on every 10-year row, the Re-engine and Do Nothing).
- The cost of waiting: about $0.03B on the grid, a 2050 fps at most about +0.04, and a 2050 Re-engine about +0.45.

Taken as advice:
- His A350 read moving from 30% to about 25% (doctrine, not his record). It changes no order, since the Re-engine never clears ε at any p.
- His balance-sheet tie-break.

His printed-grid Meet-and-beat result goes against Do Nothing by $0.07B, and I report it to the Board as he did. I resolve it on doing less first and on his own slip-priced test second.
memo_weighing.ops:
Stephanie's seat runs on operations doctrine (Very low airplane-business evidence; her record is Global Services), so I took her results as facts against the brief, not as judgement on the airplane case.

Accepted:
- The KPI gate is clean and her veto has no object.
- The four-step ladder for the MAX climb (42 / 47 / 52 / 57), gated on KPIs, FAA agreement, firm orders, and supplier output proven before 52 and 57. Adopted as an internal plan.
- Confirm the LEAP-1B allocation for 1,368 a year before the 47 step.
- Her H4 table, including the case my frame missed: a 7-year fps now with a 2050 Re-engine gives 2 years. With the slip priors, no pair has slack.
- The 2.1% overrun sensitivity, which strengthens the hold.
- Her IP test: Embraer adds no airframe IP or capacity, so via Embraer fails.
- Her five-step Renton bridge plan, carried into the 2050 case. Renton is worth 0.00 on a hold, so the site stays new_site.
- Her 2050 readiness list.

She is clear that operations does not hold the Re-engine back; the business case does. I record it that way.

boeing.expected_scenario:
S1 (rivals hold).
- No A350 Re-engine has come since 2030, and Airbus repeats that its widebody focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. Malave's doctrine read puts an A350 Re-engine at about 25% (range 20-30%).
- S2 (Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine) is the plausible downside and the worst column on every row.

Not taken:

The hold gives up $0.74B in S1 and S3 and saves $0.81B in S2. It is logged separately as a Board hold.
boeing.premium_reason:
Soft doctrine premium against the $2B cap: $0.07B. Objective premium: $0.

fps hold ($0.07B, doctrine)
- Gives up $0.07B in every column against the 10-year at Renton (-0.94 / -1.27 / -0.94).
- Reason: doing less within ε [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548].
- What breaks the number: a slip cost above about $1.0B on the +3-year clean-sheet prior (Malave), or an overrun above about 2.1% (Pope). The hold then becomes a saving.

787 Re-engine hold (logged separately as a Board hold, not against the cap)
- The binding reason is the Board's +$1B business-case line. My own ε rule and Malave's worst-column tie-break pick the hold too.
- Known cost: $0.74B given up in S1 and S3, $0.81B saved in S2.
- Weighted: $0.35B at Malave's 25% ($0.43B at 20%, $0.28B at 30%).
- What breaks the number: an A350 Re-engine turns the hold into a saving of $0.81B and closes the Re-engine for good under H3.
- Counted as soft instead, the total would be $0.81B, still inside $2B. The classification changes no decision.

Objective premium: $0. No launch this round moves a scored year: the earliest fps EIS is 2052, and every plan shows one engine source in 2050.
boeing.objective_note:
The company objectives are the company's mission, not on my ranked list. They never change the payoff, and no PV is given up for them this round.

Met:
- repair the balance sheet (2029), and keep it repaired in base and stress at every check year;
- three narrowbody engine makers in the market in 2045 and 2050.

Not met:
- hold the 50/50 split and defend incumbency (worst year 20.0%; 2045 and 2050 at 20.0%);
- dual or triple sources on our narrowbody (the 737 MAX flies CFM only, 1 source in 2040, 2045 and 2050).

No order this round can move a scored year: an fps launched now enters service in 2052 or later, and every plan shows 1 engine source in 2050.

The long-cycle stake is real but unscored: under the lead-edge rule the long-run split is 32-35% for a launch now and 27-30% for a 2050 launch. That goes into the 2050 case as information, not as a reason to waive the Board's +$1B line.

The engine-sourcing requirement is updated to code 7 (CFM plus the Joint Venture, two sources), so the enabler is ready whenever the airplane is.

ENGINE MAKERS

OUR RESULTS IF NOBODY MOVES AGAIN
- ΔPV -1.01 (S1), -1.34 (S2), -1.01 (S3); -1.09 weighted at 25% for S2.

2050

- I will bring the pair together under H4, priced with the slip, and say so plainly if it does not clear.

board_response.recommendation: Hold the fps this round, give no fps date, say plainly what has changed, carry the staged case forward, and set out the cost of waiting under the lead-edge rule as information.
board_response.response:
Taken in full.
- fps: hold, with no date in the public statement. It says the market case is better but not there yet.
- The staged case goes to 2050 as a private move: authority to offer first, the 10-year ramp, Renton with Pope's bridge plan, code 7, and item values in S1-S3 against both your lines with Malave's slip leg priced.
- What has changed: the 10-year at Renton is +0.07 in every column, about $0.51B real, from demand above both makers' slots from 2047.
- Cost of waiting: about $0.03B on the grid. The long-run split falls from 32% (10-year now) or 35% (7-year now) to 27% or 30% (2050 launches).
- Said candidly: the fps may never clear your line on this demand path. It is information, not a reason to waive the +$1B line.

board_response.recommendation: Log any objective premium against the $2B cap; note that a launch this round moves no scored year and a premium does not change the item value.
board_response.response:
Taken. The objective premium is $0, and the soft total is $0.07B (the fps hold, doctrine).
- Every plan shows 1 engine source in 2050.
- The earliest fps EIS is 2052.
- The unmet objectives (50/50, incumbency, dual source) are recorded in objective_note.
The long-cycle stake will be answered with a case that clears your tests, not with a premium.

board_response.recommendation: Hold the 787 Re-engine, log its known cost separately as a Board hold; re-test in 2050 only if H3's second half is open, sequenced under H4.
board_response.response:
Taken. re787 is hold, logged separately: $0.74B given up in S1 and S3, $0.81B saved in S2, and $0.35B weighted at Malave's 25%.
- Recorded candidly: your 2035 Downside condition is now met (worst -0.81), but the case shrank from 2.01 to 0.74 by discounting alone. My ε rule and Malave's worst-column tie-break pick the hold too.
- H3's second half is confirmed open.
- A 2050 re-test, at about +0.45, happens only if H3 is still open, decided as one pair with any fps under H4. Both held to 2050 gives 2 years with a 10-year fps and 5 with a 7-year.

board_response.recommendation: Show S3 against Do Nothing with Malave's buffer number, his Fundable result, the net-debt line, and S2 as advice; do not subtract the penalty again.
board_response.response:
Taken.
- Submitted row (Do Nothing): S3 -1.01 against a line of -3.01, so the gap is 0.00 and headroom +2.00. Buffer: pass.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass. The 777X has been cash-positive since 2029, and the gate is met for any 10-year row.
- Net debt: '2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B)' in all three columns.
- S2, the worst column: -1.34.
The penalty is netted in the grid and is not subtracted again.

board_response.recommendation: Pope's memo as the production and safety test: KPI gate, capacity, suppliers, strain, the KPI-gated MAX climb, a bridge plan if Renton, no production-certification concurrency.
board_response.response:
Taken.
- KPI gate: clean.
- MAX climb: Pope's ladder (42 / 47 / 52 / 57 a month), each step after 2-3 stable KPI months, FAA agreement and firm orders. Supplier output is proven before 52 and 57, and the LEAP-1B allocation for 1,368 a year is confirmed before 47. No launch is stacked on it.
- Strain: zero with both held.
- Site: no Renton this round. Her five-step bridge plan goes into the 2050 case.
- No production-certification concurrency: the type certificate comes before rate on any programme.

board_response.recommendation: Update the public engine-sourcing requirement: code 7 now gives two sources (CFM plus the Joint Venture), dateless, durability before EIS.
board_response.response: Taken as a public move and in the public statement: a choice of two engine sources at launch, CFM and the P&W-RR Joint Venture, with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition. It is dateless, with no launch commitment. No code is selected this round (null), because nothing is launched.

board_response.recommendation: Cash: allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board; keep headroom for a staged fps; no dividend or buyback signal.
board_response.response: Taken. There is no shareholder-return signal in the public statement. A private move keeps headroom for a staged fps: $60.32B on the 10-year ramp, about $8.44B in its peak year, which is 61% of base and 92% of stress free cash flow. The surplus decision stays with the Board.

board_response.recommendation: Do not let Airbus set our dates; decide on our own market, technology and balance-sheet readiness.
board_response.response: Taken. The hold rests on our own three work streams [BX-1296]: technology ready, balance sheet ready, and the market turning but not turned. It also rests on doing less within ε [BX-1239] and the slip pricing. Neither the hold nor the public statement cites NGSA, the Alt plan or any A350 move as a reason [B-2313].

priorities: Safety and production readiness first. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem, and the 737 holds at 57 a month. We still approve no launch without Pope's KPI, engineering, supplier and two-front-strain results. Her memo must also cover the MAX's climb back to full output in 2045-47 (deliveries of 521, then 618, then 684 a year). That climb should be KPI-gated, agreed with the FAA, and not stacked on a same-year launch without her strain result. Renton comes only with her MAX bridge plan [BG-0043, BG-0025, B-2236, BG-0069].

One well-founded launch, not a bet. For the first time the fps item value is positive in every column: +0.07 / +0.07 / +0.07 for the 10-year ramp at Renton, up from -1.20 in 2035. Ten years of discounting alone would have moved it only to -0.44, so about $0.51B of the gain is real. It is still $0.93B short of our +$1B business-case line. A result within ε of Do Nothing is a tie, and a tie goes to doing less. The 10-year at the new site is -0.08 in every column [BG-0021, BG-0022, B-0581, BG-0068, B-2303, BX-1239].

The balance sheet stays repaired. The plan must sit within $2B of Do Nothing in the risk-case column S3 (Do Nothing -1.01, so the line is -3.01). Every Solo row passes, and every via-Embraer row fails (-4.68 to -5.13). Net debt stays at $0 in base and stress on every 10-year row, on the 7-year at Renton without the Re-engine, and on the Re-engine alone. The stress case fails on the 7-year at the new site ($0.7B), on every 7-year row with the Re-engine ($2.0-3.1B) and on every via-Embraer row (advice, not a veto ground) [BG-0029, BG-0062, B-2327, BG-0034, B-2259].

One development at a time, and the 787 Re-engine judged on its own case. On its own it is +0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74. For the first time its worst column is within our -$1B line, but its expected-column value is now below the +$1B business-case line. That value is exactly its 2035 value discounted ten years (2.01 / 1.105^10 = 0.74). With a 10-year fps it falls to -1.06 in S2. With a 7-year fps it is -1.27 in S2, and the two overlap by 5 years [BG-0066, B-2167, BX-0410, BG-0022].

Decide on Boeing's own case, never as a reply to Airbus. NGSA has been in service since 2037. Its Alt plan and any A350 move are read from the bulletin only. Neither a launch nor a hold should give them as its reason [B-2313, B-2315, BG-0068].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: 4.5 of 5, unchanged since 2030, with horizon 3: (1) no Board item may lose more than $1B against its default in any plausible column, and S1-S3 all count because the bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine and Delay Tactics are covert; (2) a launch needs more than +$1B in the expected column; (3) the plan must sit within $2B of Do Nothing in risk-case column S3 (line -3.01). Net debt has been $0 since 2029 in base and stress, so the binding limits this round are the business-case and per-item lines, not the rating. The fps gets no extra allowance for its long-term position.

frame.situation:
Round 3, decision year 2045. We have launched nothing. We are on today's products: the 737 MAX with a ceiling of 57 a month (684 a year), and the 787.

**Public record**
- NGSA has been in service since 2037, with CFM, P&W and RR on it. Airbus confirmed its Alt plan at the 2035 gate, so A320 lines are kept longer.
- P&W and RR formed the Joint Venture in 2035. GTF2 and UltraFan NB folded into it, and its engine has been ready since 2036.
- CFM's ducted engine has been ready since 2041. The CFM-Embraer partnership has been ready since 2042.
- No A350 Re-engine is on the record. Airbus says its widebody focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. RR says there will be no widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. So H3's second half has not closed the 787 Re-engine.

**Market on Do Nothing (S1 -1.01: narrowbody operating profit -3.64, offset by +2.63 from supply and demand)**
- Preference share has been 20% since 2043.
- Delivered share fell to 26.6-29.9% in 2041-45. It returns to 36.3% from 2047, because Airbus's capacity of about 1,200 a year binds and its flexible customers take our free slots.
- MAX deliveries: 458 (2044), 521 (2045), 618 (2046), then 684 from 2047. That is a climb from about 43 to 51.5 to 57 a month, inside today's ceiling. It is not a Rate Increase.
- From 2047, new demand runs above both makers' slots: 1,976 against 684 + 1,200 = 1,884 in 2047, and 2,232 against 1,884 in 2050.
- That is what moved the fps item. It was -1.20 in 2035. Ten years of discounting alone would make that -0.44; it is now +0.07, so about $0.51B of the gain is real.
- The Re-engine's 2.01 in 2035, discounted ten years, is exactly its +0.74 today. Its case has not grown.

**Balance sheet**
- Net debt has been $0 since 2029, in base and stress, through 2060. Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year.
- Profit is $0.63B below the game baseline in 2045 and back to baseline by 2050. Allocating the surplus is the Board's call.

**Objectives**
- Balance-sheet lines: all met.
- 50/50 split and incumbency: not met (worst year 20%).
- Three narrowbody engine makers in the market: met.
- Two or more sources on our own narrowbody: not met (the MAX flies CFM only). Every plan shows 1 source in 2050, because the earliest fps EIS is 2052. No launch this round moves any scored year.

**KPIs.** The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. rate_737 is hold only.

**Grid columns**

  - S3 against Do Nothing (line -3.01);

  - net debt in base and stress;

frame.initial_lean:
**Do Nothing on every lever:** fps hold, fps_site new_site, fps_engine_code null, re787 hold, rate_737 hold.

**Why**
- On my four questions:
  - The KPIs are clean.
  - Technology is ready: CFM and the Joint Venture are both ready.
  - Our balance sheet is ready: net debt $0 since 2029.
  - The market leg is turning, but it hasn't turned. 'We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready' [BX-1296].
- No plan beats Do Nothing by more than ε in my expected column, S1. The best is the Re-engine alone at +0.74, then 10-year at Renton + Re-engine at +0.56, then the 10-year at Renton at +0.07.
- Within ε, doing less and doing it better wins [BX-1239], and so does the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]. Do Nothing has nothing to execute. The 10-year's +0.07 rests on a 2055 EIS with no slip priced.
- The Board would veto every launch on its +$1B line, and I have no override. Bringing an item I know it will veto is not proof before commitment [BG-0021].
- Building a new future is on my list [BX-1245]. Chasing share is not. A launch now buys none of the scored objectives, because EIS 2055 is after 2050.

**Premiums**
- fps hold: $0.07B, doctrine, logged against the cap.
- Re-engine hold: $0.74B given up in S1 and S3, $0.81B saved in S2, $0.28B weighted at 30%. Logged separately as a Board hold. I note that my own ε rule picks the hold too.
- I'll say plainly that the hold probably closes the Re-engine. It decays inside ε, and a 2050 launch meets any 2050 fps under H4.

**Close**
- Every 7-year row: 0.88-0.93 below the 10-year, with stress failures, and H4 with the Re-engine.
- Every via-Embraer row: Malave's buffer binds.

**What would move me**
- Malave or Pope finding something in the brief that puts a launch more than ε ahead in S1 with no column below -$1B. Nothing on this grid does.
- A live problem would only confirm the hold.

**For 2050**
- Bring the staged case: authority to offer first, the 10-year ramp, Renton with Pope's bridge plan, code 7, and durability before EIS.
- Test it against both lines and the slip leg.
- If it doesn't clear, I'll say so and not force it.

**Public statement**
- No fps date.
- What's changed, said plainly: the case is improving but it isn't there.
- Engine requirement updated: code 7 means CFM plus the Joint Venture, two sources.
- The MAX climb back to 57, gated on KPIs with the FAA.
- No dividend or buyback signal.
- No reason that cites Airbus [B-2313].

'I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned' [BX-1300]. And it is still more important that we do this right than fast [BX-1241].

Kelly, I ran the buffer as the baseline: S3 no worse than -3.01, $2B under Do Nothing's -1.01. Your list is right. Every Solo row passes, the 7-year at new sites by only $0.99B. Every via-Embraer row fails, $1.67-2.12B past the line, and that veto binds.

The 787 Re-engine is +0.74 at best, inside ε whatever the odds of an A350 move. My read is now about 25%, worth $0.35B. Log it as a Board hold.

The cost of waiting, honestly: about $0.03B on this board, plus share after 2050 the grid can't price. Nothing in the brief puts a 2050 launch above +$1B. That is information, not a reason.

So 100% of every plan's value survives Delay Tactics: they move preference, and from 2047 our 684 slots are full anyway. The risk-case column prices no slip, and S2 is the worst column on every row.

Slip sensitivity (inference: discounting at the 10.5% WACC only). Each year of later EIS takes about 9.5% off a programme's value.
- 787 Re-engine on the derivative prior (+2 years, range +1 to +4): +0.74 becomes +0.67 at +1, +0.61 at +2 and +0.50 at +4.
- fps 10-year at Renton on the clean-sheet prior (+3 years, range +2 to +5): EIS 2055 becomes 2058 central. Discounting alone takes +0.07 to +0.05. The slip also costs 3 pp of long-run split under the lead-edge rule (32% to 29%), which the grid cannot price.
- fps cost: the bill is booked in 2055 at a PV factor of 18.09. Each 1% overrun on $60.32B costs about $0.033B of PV, so a 2.1% overrun (about $1.27B) erases the +0.07, before any added debt penalty. The fps value depends wholly on the nominal date and the nominal bill.

The recommended plan (hold) has no EIS to deliver. Its delivery commitment is the MAX climb back (521, 618 and 684 a year in 2045-47), and my ladder below delivers it inside doctrine. Result: pass for the hold. A launch on this grid would not be predictable.

tests.name: KPI gate (doctrine; my veto) - answers the CEO's ask 1
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of +5 a month or less, at least 6 months apart, each after 2-3 stable months on the six FAA-agreed KPIs and an FAA review. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. The menu offers only rate_737: hold, because the Rate Increase was a 2030-only order. My veto therefore has neither a ground nor an object, and I do not invoke it.

Watch items, not live problems on our line:
- CFM says publicly that LEAP durability kits and deliveries come first, and that it fixes its supply base before it loads it. The LEAP-1B is our sole MAX engine.
- P&W's GTF powder-metal and shop-capacity issues are on the A320neo, not the MAX.

The MAX built 684 a year to plan in 2030-36. Deliveries of 409-468 a year in 2038-44 were limited by demand, not by a production problem.

tests.name: MAX climb back 2045-47, KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA (doctrine) - answers ask 2
tests.threshold: Each step is +5 a month or less, at least 6 months apart, after 2-3 stable months and FAA agreement. Supplier output (above all LEAP-1B) is proven before each break. No step is stacked on a same-year launch without the strain result.
tests.numbers:
Board deliveries: 458 in 2044 (38.2 a month), 521 in 2045 (43.4), 618 in 2046 (51.5), then 684 from 2047 (57). This is inside today's 57-a-month ceiling and is not a Rate Increase. On the floor, though, it is a climb of 19 a month, so I gate it like one.

Ladder: 38, then 42 (Jan 2045), 47 (Oct 2045), 52 (Apr 2046) and 57 (Oct 2046). That is four steps of +4 or +5, 6-9 months apart. It builds 519 / 624 / 684 against the board's 521 / 618 / 684, within 1%.

Gates at each step:
- 2-3 stable months on the six KPIs, then FAA agreement. A month late rather than a month early.
- Supplier output proven before the 52 and 57 steps. Beyond 47 the supply chain binds [B-2340], and the 2018 step to 52 broke Spirit and CFM supply [B-1449].

LEAP-1B: 916 engines (2044), then 1,042, 1,236 and 1,368 a year by 2047, before spares. That is +452 (+49%). In 2044 the MAX took about 54% of CFM's narrowbody engines (49.6% of 3,448, about 1,710). CFM also carries NGSA, the A320neo on the Alt plan, its ducted engine and Embraer. Confirm the allocation for 1,368 a year before the 47 step.

Demand check: the rival's flexible customers taking our free slots are 31% of MAX deliveries in 2045 (160 of 521) and 42% in 2047 (289 of 684). Gate each step on firm orders, not on the board's forecast.

Same-year fps launch:
- On the board, a 10-year fps's strain window opens in 2048. That is after the ladder reaches 57 (Oct 2046). Year-1 spend is about $3.0B.
- A 7-year fps's window opens in 2045, on top of the climb.
- On the supply base, any launch puts new-part sourcing on the same suppliers that must carry 47, 52 and 57 (inference).

So a 7-year launch is two fronts. A 10-year launch can be sequenced, but not for free.

tests.name: Two-front strain / engineering capacity (doctrine) - answers ask 3
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain = $3B x overlap / 5. The fps window runs from EIS-7 to EIS, the Re-engine window from EIS-5 to EIS.
tests.numbers:
Recommended plan (both on hold): 0 years, $0, nothing in development.

Same round (2045), confirmed:
- 10-year fps (2048-55) + Re-engine (2045-50): 2 years (2048-50), $1.2B, at the limit with no slack.
- 7-year fps (2045-52) + Re-engine: 5 years, $3.0B. That is an H4 breach.

Across rounds:
- 10-year fps now + a 2050 Re-engine (2050-55): 5 years, a breach. Confirmed.
- 7-year fps now + a 2050 Re-engine: 2 years (2050-52), at the limit. This case is not in the frame's list.
- Re-engine now + a 2050 fps: 0 years (7-year window 2050-57, 10-year 2053-60). Confirmed.
- Both held to 2050: 2 years with a 10-year fps (2053-55), 5 years with a 7-year. Confirmed.

Slip priors (doctrine): derivative +2 years (range +1 to +4), clean-sheet +3 (range +2 to +5). Engineering starts at launch, and a slip extends the end:
- same-round 10-year fps + Re-engine: 3 years at +1, and 4 years ($2.4B) at +2, past H4;
- both held to 2050 with a 10-year fps: 4 years at +2, past H4;
- Re-engine now + a 2050 10-year fps: 0 years at +2, 1 at +4;
- Re-engine now + a 2050 7-year fps: 2 years at +2, 4 at +4.

No fps and Re-engine pair sits at the limit with slack. This is information, not a case for either launch.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year (inference)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably with the workforce and suppliers in the brief? State the strain and EIS of each.
tests.numbers:
No fps this round.

A 2045 launch:
- 7-year: EIS 2052, central 2055 on the clean-sheet prior (range 2054-57).
- 10-year: EIS 2055, central 2058 (range 2057-60).

Strain is $0 for either alone. With a same-round Re-engine it is $3.0B for the 7-year (a breach) and $1.2B for the 10-year (the limit).

The 10-year beats the 7-year in every column: by 0.93 (new site) and 0.88 (Renton) on the hold rows, and by 1.14 and 1.08 with the Re-engine. It also has the higher worst column.

Stress-case net debt is $0 on every 10-year row. The 7-year fails at new sites ($0.7B) and with the Re-engine ($2.0-3.1B). Its strain window (2045-52) also lands on the MAX climb.

If an fps is ever brought, operations backs only the 10-year. A 2050 launch would enter service in 2057 (7-year) or 2060 (10-year).

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP (record [BX-1330, BX-1333], applied to airplanes by inference) - answers ask 5
tests.threshold: fps Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds IP or capacity Boeing lacks, at a cost within $1B of Solo.

tests.name: Engine and supplier readiness by a 2052 or 2055 EIS (doctrine; supplier readiness is a hard gate) - answers ask 4
tests.threshold: Each named engine maker is ready by EIS, with durability proven before EIS. Supplier output meets the rate before each rate break. A sole source is a risk to reduce.
tests.numbers:
The engine code is null with the hold.

At any launch, code 7. The brief's table gives 2 fitted sources at a 2055 EIS: CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture. Codes 5 and 6 also give 2; codes 1-4 give 1.

Readiness:
- The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036: 16 years before a 2052 EIS and 19 before 2055.
- CFM's ducted engine has been ready since 2041.
- Durability proven before EIS is a contract condition [BX-1298]. The Joint Venture's first configuration is GTF2's tested one, and P&W puts fleet spares ahead of new-engine test hardware. So the item to watch is the durability evidence, not the date.

Today 100% of MAX engines are CFM: 1,368 LEAP-1B a year at 57 a month. Every plan shows 1 source in 2050.

Supplier output before each rate break [B-2308]: the brief has no supplier data, so this is a gate at each break, not a fail.

tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness for a 2045 launch, EIS 2050 (doctrine) - answers ask 7
tests.threshold: Engineering is free, Charleston has capacity, the engine is ready with durability proven, the supplier gate is met on new parts, and the type certificate comes before building at rate.
tests.numbers:
Engineering: nothing is in development, so a Re-engine would be the one development.

Engine: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033. RR says there will be no widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. At 6 years from launch it could not be ready before 2051, after a 2050 EIS, so the date rests on the GEnx.

Charleston: the footprint covers 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. The 787 builds 100 a year (8.3 a month). A lone Re-engine gaining 1 pp a year from 58.8% reaches about 108 a year (9.0 a month) in 2055, 117 (9.7) in 2060 and 144 (12.0) at the 85% cap.

Supplier gate on new parts, as on the 787 heat exchangers [B-2308]: a condition at the rate break.

Certification: the type certificate comes before building at rate.

Central EIS on the derivative prior: 2052.

H3, second half, confirmed open: no A350 Re-engine is on the public record. Airbus says its widebody focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F.

Operations does not hold the Re-engine back. It fails the Board's +$1B line at +0.74, which is a business-case test, not a readiness one.

tests.name: No production-certification concurrency (doctrine)
tests.threshold: The type certificate comes before building at rate on any new airframe or derivative. No Renton conversion before the fps type certificate.

tests.name: Renton or new site, with the MAX bridge plan (inference) - answers ask 6
tests.threshold: Renton only alongside a launch, with a MAX bridge plan so that the Renton wind-down follows the fps's actual ramp. Otherwise new_site.
tests.numbers:
With a hold, Renton is worth 0.00 in every column, so keep new_site. There is no reason to set the site before a launch:
- the site can change in any round before EIS;
- the full ~$3.0B capex saving needs only a choice 3 years before EIS. That is by 2052 for a 2055 EIS, and a 2050 launch (EIS 2057 or 2060) still captures it in full.

With a launch, Renton is worth +0.15 (10-year) or +0.20 to +0.21 (7-year).

The risk is sharper than in 2035. From 2047 all 684 MAX slots are full, and Renton carries 47 of the 57 a month. If Renton converts ahead of the fps's actual ramp, the MAX falls to the Everett North Line at up to 15 a month (180 a year). That is a gap of up to 504 aircraft a year, and each one is a lost delivery.

Bridge plan, when Renton is chosen:
1. No Renton line converts before the fps type certificate.
2. Each Renton MAX line comes down only after the fps line has held its rate for 2-3 stable KPI months.
3. One Renton MAX line stays warm until the fps reaches about 50 a month, about 4 years after EIS.
4. The LEAP-1B allocation and MAX suppliers follow the actual wind-down, not the planned one.
5. The Everett North Line carries the tail, at up to 15 a month.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand (inference, one remark [BX-1329])
tests.threshold: Back a Rate Increase where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column. Otherwise, not applicable.
tests.numbers:
There are no Rate Increase rows on this grid (it was a 2030-only order).

Demand above capacity is visible for the first time since the 2033 backlog peak (1,319 waiting). New demand runs above both makers' slots (684 + 1,200) by 92 in 2047, 348 in 2050, 416 in 2053, 390 in 2055 and 245 in 2060.

Our own preference demand (395-460 a year) stays below our 684 slots. From 2047, 224-289 of those 684 a year are the rival's flexible customers.

That excess moved the fps item, about $0.51B of it real. The only capacity lever on the board is the fps, from 2055. It is the signal to prepare the 2050 case, not to add capacity now.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record [BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option, when the bill lands and what it does to cash and net debt, as numbers rather than adjectives.
tests.numbers:
Base free cash flow is $13.79B a year ($9.19B in stress). Profit is $0.63B below baseline in 2045 and back to baseline by 2050.

- Do Nothing: no bill. Net debt $0 in base and stress to 2060.
- Re-engine: $5B over 2045-50, about $1.0B a year (7% of base, 11% of stress), booked in 2050 (PV $0.46B), with a $0.6B undiscounted penalty. It returns +$148M of PV per $1B of bill in S1 and S3, and -$162M in S2. Net debt $0.
- fps 10-year: $60.32B over 2045-55. Year 1 is about $3.02B (22% of base, 33% of stress). The peak is about $8.44B in year 7, around 2051 (61% / 92%). Booked in 2055. It returns about +$1.2M of PV per $1B at Renton and -$1.3M at new sites: no return on the capital. Net debt $0.
- 10-year + Re-engine: both bills in 2045-50, plus $1.2B of strain in 2048-50. Net debt $0.
- fps 7-year: $65.00B over 2045-52, about $9.3B a year (67% / 101%). It returns -$12.5M per $1B at Renton. Stress fails at new sites ($0.7B).
- Via Embraer: a peak of about $14.0B (102% / 152%). Stress fails ($1.5-6.3B).

Renton saves ~$3.0B of capex, and only with a launch.

tests.name: 2050 readiness: workforce, production system, suppliers, Renton bridge (doctrine and inference) - answers ask 8
tests.threshold: What has to happen in 2045-50 so that, if the 2050 case clears, Boeing goes on day one.
tests.numbers:
There is no order here; this is the plan.
1. Workforce: the climb from 38 to 57 a month brings back the trained people kept through the 2038-44 dip. Train for the ladder first. Then form a protected fps production-system team that does not draw on the line.
2. Production system: design the fps line with the airplane, and prove it at rate before authority to offer. The type certificate comes before rate.
3. Suppliers: keep fragile suppliers funded through the climb, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources. The suppliers that carry 52 and 57 are the ones a 2050 fps loads next.
4. Engines: refresh the code-7 proposals (CFM plus the Joint Venture), with durability evidence before EIS.
5. Renton bridge: write it now and decide it with the launch.
6. H4: if both stay held to 2050, a 10-year fps and a 2050 Re-engine overlap by 2 years (4 on slip), and a 7-year fps by 5. Decide the pair together in 2050.
7. Use the time the way we used the strike: stability first, then go.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (KPI veto NOT invoked)
vetoes.ground: No Rate Increase is on the menu (it was a 2030-only order), and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. The KPI doctrine has neither a ground nor an object this round, so it is not invoked. As doctrine advice, not a board order, the same gate applies to each step of the 2045-47 MAX climb: no step while a KPI is out, or while LEAP-1B or supplier output is short of the next rate.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag H4, not my veto. The overlap is 5 years (fps 2045-52, Re-engine 2045-50), with $3.0B of strain undiscounted, past the 2-year limit. The CEO must strike it.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_10yr now, with the 787 Re-engine held for a 2050 launch
vetoes.ground: H4 flag across rounds, not a breach this round. A 2050 Re-engine (2050-55) would overlap a 2045 10-year fps (2048-55) by 5 years, $3.0B. A 10-year fps launched now therefore closes the 2050 Re-engine under H4.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_10yr with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a breach on the board. The overlap is 2 years (2048-50) with $1.2B of strain, at the limit with no slack. It becomes 3 years on a 1-year derivative slip and 4 years ($2.4B) on the 2-year central prior. Beside the fps, the Re-engine item falls to +0.49 / -1.06 / +0.49.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr (any row)
vetoes.ground: Operations advice. Its strain window (2045-52) lands on the MAX climb from day one. It sits 0.88-1.14 below the 10-year in every column. Stress-case net debt fails at new sites ($0.7B) and with the Re-engine ($2.0-3.1B).

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer
vetoes.ground: IP advice, not binding. On the board the partner brings no IP, capacity or strain relief. It has the same EIS as the Solo 10-year and sits $4.04-4.23B below it in every column, with a $52.5B undiscounted debt penalty. Stress-case net debt fails ($1.5-6.3B). Malave's buffer, not my seat, binds against it.

vetoes.plan: fps_site: renton without a launch, or with a launch but no MAX bridge plan
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding. Without a launch Renton is worth 0.00. With a launch it needs the five-step bridge plan in my memo. From 2047 all 684 MAX slots are full, so a conversion ahead of the fps's actual ramp leaves the MAX on the Everett North Line at up to 180 a year, a gap of up to 504 deliveries a year.

ops.memo:
Three results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes, so the KPI, supplier and strain gates run on operations doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. The KPI gate is clean, and my veto has nothing to act on. The 2045 job is the MAX climb from 38 to 57 a month: 42 now, 47 in October, 52 next April, 57 next October. Each step is KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA. That builds 519, 624 and 684 against the board's 521, 618 and 684. It needs 452 more LEAP-1B engines a year by 2047, up 49%, and suppliers proven before 52, the step that broke supply in 2018.

Second, engineering capacity. Holding both gives zero strain and one front, the climb. A 7-year fps lands on the climb from day one. A 10-year fps with the Re-engine sits at H4's 2-year limit, and reaches 4 years on a 2-year derivative slip.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth. The 10-year fps at Renton returns about $1 million of value per $1 billion of bill. A 2% overrun on $60.32 billion erases it, and our clean-sheet prior is a 3-year slip. The Re-engine returns $148 million per billion in S1 and loses $162 million in S2. Embraer adds no IP or capacity we lack, at $4.04-4.23 billion below Solo.

Orders: fps hold, new_site, no code; Re-engine hold. Operations does not hold the Re-engine back. The business case does.

other_moves.move: Staged fps business case for the 2050 round (authority-to-offer work)
other_moves.detail:
Solo by default. Pope's IP test finds that Embraer brings no airframe IP or capacity we lack: its partnership is with CFM, and via Embraer sits $4.04-4.23B below the Solo 10-year.

The base case is the 10-year ramp. It beats the 7-year by 0.88-1.14 in every column, has the higher worst column, and holds stress net debt at $0.

Renton only with Pope's five-step MAX bridge plan:
1. No conversion before the fps type certificate.
2. Each Renton line comes down only after the fps line has held rate for 2-3 stable KPI months.
3. One Renton MAX line stays warm until the fps reaches about 50 a month.
4. The LEAP-1B allocation follows the actual wind-down.
5. The Everett North Line carries the tail at up to 15 a month.

Code 7 (CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture), with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition. Design the production system with the airplane and prove it at rate before authority to offer. Type certificate before rate; no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].

The case must show:
- the item value in S1, S2 and S3 against the Board's two lines;
- Malave's slip leg as the baseline, with the clean-sheet prior (+3 years) and a cost-overrun sensitivity (does the item survive a 2% overrun?) priced in full, once;
- the cost of waiting under the public lead-edge rule.

Decide the fps and the 787 Re-engine together, as one pair, under H4: both held to 2050 gives 2 years with a 10-year fps and 5 with a 7-year. If the 2050 case does not clear, we say so and do not force it.

other_moves.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle (updated to the record)
other_moves.detail: We continue to invite the narrowbody engine makers to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. With GTF2 and UltraFan NB now folded into the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, our plan at launch is a choice of two engine sources: CFM and the Joint Venture (code 7). Selection is on value among engines actually launched, with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition. No fps date and no launch commitment.

other_moves.move: 737 MAX back to full output at 57 a month, KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA
other_moves.detail: As demand comes back, the 737 returns to its 57-a-month ceiling. This is not a Rate Increase. Each step is taken one at a time, only after stable KPIs and agreement with the FAA, and only when supplier and engine output for the next step is proven. No step dates are published.

other_moves.move: MAX climb-back ladder and supplier gates (internal plan)
Keep the trained workforce and fragile suppliers funded through the climb
other_moves.detail: Bring back the trained people kept through the 2038-44 dip, and train for the ladder first. Then form a protected fps production-system team that does not draw on the line. Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources [BX-1243, B-2330]. The suppliers that carry 52 and 57 are the ones a 2050 fps would load next.

other_moves.move: 787 Re-engine: study only, no launch
other_moves.detail:
Engine basis: the GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033. Recorded candidly: the item has shrunk by ten years of discounting (2.01 in 2035 to 0.74 now), and a 2050 launch is about +0.45, below ε at any probability of an A350 Re-engine. This hold very probably closes it on this board.

Re-test it in 2050 only if H3's second half is still open (no A350 Re-engine on the record), and only as one pair with any fps under H4. No programme spend is committed.

other_moves.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
other_moves.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

other_moves.move: No shareholder-return signal
other_moves.detail: Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress. Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board. Keep headroom for a staged fps ($60.32B on the 10-year ramp, about $8.44B in its peak year, 92% of stress free cash flow). Nothing is said publicly.

decision.public_statement:
Five years ago I said I thought we'd turned the ship. We have, and the job now is to keep it steady. The balance sheet is repaired and it's staying repaired. The 777X and the 737 MAX family are delivering, and the 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class.

On the 737, we're bringing the line back to full output, 57 a month, as demand comes back. We'll take that one step at a time. Each step comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity, and when we and the FAA agree the line is ready. We'll make sure our suppliers and our engine supply are there before each step. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early.

On a new airplane: we're not launching one this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. I'll tell you plainly what's changed. The market case is better than it was. It isn't there yet. We will do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing are all ready. Technology is ready, and Boeing is ready. The market is getting there, but it hasn't got there. The work goes on in stages. We're designing the production system together with the airplane, so that when we go, we go on a conservative plan with headroom in it, with no fixed-price development risk, and we build it at rate the right way.

On engines, we've updated our requirement. Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are now one Joint Venture, so our plan is to give customers a choice of two engine sources at launch, CFM and the Joint Venture, with durability proven before entry into service.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year. We'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

Our dates are set by our own readiness. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every lever. fps hold, fps_site new_site, fps_engine_code null, re787 hold, rate_737 hold.
- Submitted row: -1.01 / -1.34 / -1.01 (S1 / S2 / S3).
- Nothing differs from the default, so there is no Board item.

TEAM RULE
- Malave's buffer veto binds on all four via-Embraer rows (S3 -4.68 to -5.13, 1.67-2.12 past the -3.01 line). None is chosen.
- The KPI doctrine has no object: rate_737 is hold only, and no problem is live.
- Pope flagged H4 on the 7-year fps + Re-engine (5 years) and on a 10-year fps now with a 2050 Re-engine (5 years). Neither is chosen.
- No flag needs a strike, and there are no overrides.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. KPIs stable? Yes. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem [BX-1271]. The FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
2. Market, technology and Boeing all ready [BX-1296, BX-1305]?
   - Technology: yes. CFM is always ready, and the Joint Venture has been ready since 2036.
   - Balance sheet: yes. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 in base and stress, the 777X turned in 2029 [BX-0547], and Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' gate passes for any 10-year row.
   - Market: turning, not turned. Demand above both makers' slots from 2047 moved the fps item from -1.20 to +0.07, about $0.51B of it real. That is still a tie, not a case [BX-1300].
3. What if certification takes longer? S3 equals S1 on every row, so the printed slip leg prices nothing. Malave priced the slip instead:
   - fps: on the clean-sheet prior of +3 years, any slip cost above about $1.0B (1.7% of the bill) turns the 10-year at Renton negative. The 777X reset alone was $4.9B [BX-0550].
   - Pope: a 2.1% overrun erases it on its own.
   - Re-engine: the derivative prior takes it to +0.61.
   So I plan for the reset, once [BX-1318, BX-1319], and the fps edge does not survive it.
4. Doing less, better [BX-1239]? Every plan within ε of Do Nothing in S1 (+0.74, +0.56, +0.41, +0.07, -0.08, ...) loses to doing less. Do Nothing is also the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]: it has nothing to slip.

DEBT FIRST (the grid already nets the penalty; not subtracted again)
- No plan beats Do Nothing by more than ε in S1.
- Undiscounted penalties, for scale only: 10-year $19.1B against a $0.07B netted edge; Re-engine $0.6B.

TIE-BREAK ON WORST COLUMN
Malave reports plainly that on the printed grid the 10-year at Renton has the higher worst column (S2 -1.27 against -1.34). airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s, and its production ramp-up is now reaching its planned rate. We will continue a disciplined and controlled ramp-up: every step is gated on safety, on quality and on the readiness of our supply chain, and safety and quality come before schedule. Our customers have a choice of engine, from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, and our supply agreements are matched to our own volumes. The A320neo family is completing an orderly transition to the new aircraft. Demand for the new aircraft remains strong. With our suppliers we are preparing the next step in our industrial capacity, and we will take it when our safety, quality and supply indicators say so, not before. On widebodies, our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F, which we continue to improve for our customers. We continue to secure key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. The new aircraft was funded from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
airbus.rationale:
DECISION: the company default on every lever, on our own clock.
- Orders: `ngsa: hold` (in service since 2037, engine code fixed), `rea350: hold`, `delay_tactics: none`, `a320_plan: alt`.
- Every field is at its default, so there are no Board items and no override. The game's single override stays unspent.
- The A350 Re-engine was genuinely considered at the 2045 gate and is not tabled. The tests that stopped it are named below and in `board_response`.

THE ROUND AGAINST MY PAID OBJECTIVES, IN ORDER
1. Five pillars: no order or line contradicts them (Wagner, ask 7). No safety, quality, supply-crunch or engine-slip event is on the record [AX-0073, AX-0081].
2. Ramp: NGSA delivers 1,194 aircraft in 2045 and 1,200 a year (100 a month) from 2047, and the Alt plan runs out by 2047. Our own factory ceiling, not preference, now binds. That is why I prepare a capacity step on Wagner's gates and do not commit it.
3. Airbus of the 2030s and beyond: NGSA entered service in 2037, two years after the technology-ready year, with no slip. The widebody question is the one strategic lever left. It does not clear our own launch bar this round.
4. Board: the default is never vetoed. A Re-engine tabled against an unresolved ExCo soft veto would be vetoed.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
Deleted as red lines or pillars (never traded for PV):
- Every Delay Tactics row. Under rule 4 fps is not public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
- One move on the hold row is -11.45 / -0.18 / -0.18 / -0.21 / -0.18 / -11.46 / -0.19; both moves are -11.71 to -11.72 in S1/S6. It gains in no column, even where fps launches, because our 1,200-a-year capacity binds.
- `both` is two moves. `bottleneck` and `both` fail integrity. `poaching` on the hold row breaks rule 5.
- The team's stricter condition stays in force: I record no set-aside.

Tested:
- Default: passes every Toepfer test (peak cash $0.0B against $5.2B; worst S7 +12.78; net cash rebuilt) and every Wagner test.

tests.numbers: On the hold row nothing is in development (NGSA has been in service since 2037), so `poaching` breaks rule 5. On the Re-engine row rule 5 would be met, but rule 4 (fps not public) already deletes it, and it is negative in every column (best -0.19).

tests.numbers: NGSA is in service, so it cannot be cancelled. No A350 Re-engine is live. If we launch now and Boeing re-engines the 787 in the same round (S6/S7), both enter service in 2050, so the 787 is not first and no cancel case can arise on this board.

tests.name: Net cash path since 2037, rating and returns, CEO ask 4
tests.threshold: No equity raise and no dividend cut. A+/A1 and the 30-50% payout kept fundable. Any buyback goes to the Board as a reserved matter. Net cash back to at least FY2025's EUR 12.2bn (about $13.4B)
tests.numbers: This is a proxy (inference), in 2026 prices. FCF before programme spend is held at FY2025 conversion: $5.23B / $7.6B = 0.688 of the brief's operating profit. That gives $3.85 / 4.33 / 4.82 / 5.92 / 8.26 / 9.77 / 10.73 / 12.11 / 12.45B for 2037-45, less the $0.09B Alt tail to 2044. Start: the round-2 proxy of -$0.7B at end-2036. (a) Dividend held at EUR 3.20 ($2.8B): end-2037 +$0.3B (the trough), end-2041 +$12.0B, end-2042 +$18.9B, end-2044 +$35.9B, end-2045 +$45.6B. (b) Dividend scaled with profit at a 48% payout: end-2042 +$15.9B, end-2044 +$26.3B, end-2045 +$32.1B. Net cash is back above $13.4B by 2042 on either path. With the Re-engine at $1.0B a year, end-2045 is $1.0B lower and end-2049 is +$50.1B to +$78.9B, against +$55.1B to +$83.9B on hold. Neither row needs debt or a raise, and neither cuts the dividend. A+/A1: the record gives no agency thresholds, and nothing here adds debt. My round-2 net-cash flag is cleared. Any new buyback comes to the Board as a reserved matter, with the Re-engine's $1.0B peak shown. The 2029 outlook stays upside only.

tests.name: Reported against adjusted: the $5B charge at EIS 2050, CEO ask 5

tests.numbers: On the Re-engine row the board books $5B at EIS 2050 (PV about $0.79B at 2026). The cash was spent 2045-49 at $1.0B a year, so 2050 carries a booking, not cash. Using the hold row's 2050 operating profit of $18.0B (the brief gives no 2050 profit for the Re-engine row), that is about $13.0B reported against about $18.0B underlying. The charge is shown beside the adjusted figure, not netted away. The hold row books no charge.

tests.name: Waiting: is a later Re-engine (launched 2050, EIS 2055) priced? CEO ask 6
tests.threshold: Use only numbers from the brief
tests.numbers: Nothing on the record prices it. The grid assumes nobody moves after this round, and the brief values no 2050 launch. I give no number. What the record does say: a 787 Re-engine on the record by 2050 would close it under rule 3, and any S6/S7 outcome this round does exactly that. The CEO's reading, that holding now probably means no A350 Re-engine in this game, is consistent with the record.

tests.name: Board downside (the Board's test, shown for its cash and risk read)
tests.threshold: No Board item loses more than $2B in any plausible column
tests.numbers: The Re-engine item's worst column is -0.50 (S6/S7), inside -$2B. This is the Board's test, not mine, and passing it does not clear my robustness test.

tests.name: Board cash lines, CEO ask 8
tests.threshold: Every order that differs from the default goes to the Board with its S1-S7 row, the default row and the peak-year arithmetic [AX-0026, AG-0049]
tests.numbers: DEFAULT ROW (no Board items): +13.71 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +13.61 / +12.78; worst S7 +12.78. No new programme cash. NGSA spend ended in 2036 and its $36.3B was booked in 2037. Net cash is rebuilt above FY2025's $13.4B by 2042 (proxy). Rating and the 30-50% payout are fundable with no raise and no cut; buybacks are a reserved matter. RE-ENGINE ITEM, if tabled (Qualified Majority, $5B, about EUR 4.55bn): cash $1.0B a year over 2045-49, $4.2B inside the $5.2B line, zero overlap, $0 strain. A $5B charge at EIS 2050: about $13.0B reported against $18.0B underlying. Item +0.90 / +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.89 / -0.50 / -0.50: +0.75 / +0.69 on the CEO's weights, +0.49 equal.
