vetoes.plan: `rea350: launch` (NGSA hold, Alt plan, no Delay Tactics): the CEO's test case
vetoes.ground: Failed robustness test (soft veto). Against the best passing option (hold) the item is +0.90 / +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.89 / -0.50 / -0.50: +0.75 on the CEO's round-2 weights, +0.69 refreshed, +0.49 on my equal weights. It turns negative in plausible columns S6/S7 and misses $1B in every column and on every weighting. The company's $1B launch test also fails in every column. Peak cash passes ($1.0B a year against $5.2B), so cash is not the ground. The grid margin over the best passing option is +0.90 at best, below the $1B an override needs, and on this Qualified Majority item the plan is also behind in the worst column (-0.50). I see no override that could carry it. Whether to override is the CEO's call, not mine.

vetoes.plan: Any `delay_tactics` value (`bottleneck`, `poaching` or `both`) on the hold row or the Re-engine row
vetoes.ground: Company red lines, not overridable. (1) Rule 4: fps is not on the public record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine: -11.45 to -11.47 in S1/S6 for one move, -11.71 to -11.73 for both. (2) `both` is a second move. (3) Rule 5: on the hold row nothing is in development, so `poaching` has no programme to serve. (4) Integrity pillar: I could not defend `bottleneck` or `both` to the Audit Committee. No value gains in any column (best -0.18), so no $1B case exists.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Re-engine, any one of three. (1) A grid that puts the item at least $1B over hold in the expected column, with no negative plausible column. (2) S6/S7 ruled out on the public record. The item would then be positive in every remaining column and pass my robustness test; whether to take it below $1B would be the CEO's doctrine call. A sealed round cannot give us this. (3) A Board decision. Peak cash would stop it only if programme spend rose above the $5.2B line: for example, a capacity step beyond 100 a month tabled with it, with capex above the $4.2B headroom. The net-cash verdict would change only if actual FCF ran far below my proxy of 0.69 x operating profit; the Re-engine's $1.0B a year leaves wide room. Delay Tactics: only `poaching` alone, and only with fps public and not yet in service, a programme in development, no earlier move, at least $1B in the expected column, and the CEO's recorded set-aside of the team's stricter condition. Today no value gains in any column, and the Board vetoes all of them.
cfo.memo:
2045 gate, for the Audit Committee.

Recommendation: the company default on every lever. The A350 Re-engine stays on hold, no Delay Tactics, the Alt plan runs out, NGSA stays on its ramp (engine code fixed; on engines I defer to Lars). No Board items.

Peak cash: pass on both rows. The Re-engine is $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year over 2045-49, with zero NGSA overlap and $0 strain: $4.2B inside one year's FCF (EUR 4,753m at $1.10 = $5.2B). Cash does not stop it.

Robustness: fail on the Re-engine item. Against hold it is +0.90 / +0.89 x4 / -0.50 / -0.50: +0.75 and +0.69 on the CEO's weights, +0.49 on my equal weights. It turns negative in S6/S7 and misses $1B in every column, so my soft veto is binding. No override can reach $1B, and the item trails in the worst column. The company's $1B launch test also fails in every column. The teams.md form passes: worst column S7, +12.28.

Net cash (proxy, inference): from about zero at end-2036 it is back above FY2025's $13.4B by 2042 and at $26-36B by end-2044 (2026 prices). The rating, the 30-50% payout and any buyback stay fundable with no raise and no cut, with or without the Re-engine. Buybacks remain a Board reserved matter.

Reported against adjusted: a launch books $5B at EIS 2050, about $13.0B reported against $18.0B underlying, shown, not netted.

Nothing on the record prices a 2050 launch. Delay Tactics: deleted; no column gains.

tests.name: NGSA ramp, quality and rule 1 (ask 1; Re-engine condition d)
tests.threshold: NGSA in service at or after 2035 (rule 1). A disciplined and controlled ramp to 100 a month. No open NGSA quality finding. NGSA stays on the full Board's twice-yearly product-safety review
tests.numbers:
- EIS 2037, two years after the 2035 floor.
- NGSA capacity 2037-45: 8 / 27 / 93 / 293 / 551 / 798 / 959 / 1,098 / 1,194 aircraft, which is about 1 / 2 / 8 / 24 / 46 / 67 / 80 / 92 / 99.5 a month.
- Delivered: 1,219 in 2045 (1,194 NGSA plus 25 A320), 1,200 in 2046, then 1,200 a year (100 a month) from 2047.
- The A320 Alt plan runs out by 2047 as planned. NGSA has been filled first every year.
- The brief reports no quality finding, no quality event, no supply crunch and no engine slip, and the board has no injects.
- Confirmed: NGSA stays on the full Board's twice-yearly product-safety review through the ramp and in steady state.
- The record holds proxies, not plant measurements: no KPI, escape or concession data. I report the proxy and say so.

tests.name: NGSA engine supply and the enabler; Joint Venture durability (ask 2)
tests.threshold: CFM plus at least one second source on NGSA, with three narrowbody engine makers in the market in 2045 and 2050. No engine enters service before durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life
tests.numbers:
- Fitted sources: CFM plus the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, which counts as one source. That is 2 sources from 3 makers (CFM, P&W, RR) in 2040, 2045 and 2050, on every grid row. The bulletin's 'CFM + PW + RR' is the same hardware.
- This is the cut from 3 sources to 2 that I warned of in round 2. The enabler is still met.
- The engine code is fixed (None) with NGSA in service.
- Observed narrowbody engine shares in 2044: CFM 49.6%, P&W 27.1%, RR 23.2%.
- Joint Venture durability and full-life parts: the record holds no in-service durability or life-limited-part data. The brief reports no engine slip.
- P&W's stated terms: the first Joint Venture engine in service is GTF2's tested configuration, Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block after its own durability proof, and no Joint Venture engine enters service until durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life.
- Watch item: P&W's own account of GTF time on wing (a powder-metal process issue, shop and parts capacity, hot and sandy operations). CFM, certified first, stays the backstop source.
- Our narrowbody engine demand: 2,438 engines in 2045 and 2,400 a year from 2047, across both sources.
- The CFM capacity agreements stay at our own volumes with no exclusivity. With the A320neo tail ending by 2047, they now cover essentially NGSA volumes.

tests.name: Supply crunch (asks 2 and 3e)
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch: no new concurrency (binding, never overridden)
tests.numbers:
- No crunch is reported, and the board has no injects. The test is not triggered for the default or for the A350 Re-engine.
- The waiting backlog (107 in 2045, 223 in 2047, 616 in 2050, 2,297 in 2060) and the 63.7% delivered share against 80% preference from 2047 come from our own factory ceiling at 100 a month, not from a supplier crunch.
- CFM's public line, 'we fix the supply base we have before we load it', is a watch item, not a reported crunch.

tests.name: Engineering capacity and rule 6: A350 Re-engine launched in 2045 (ask 3b)
tests.threshold: NGSA and A350 development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain) unless the grid shows at least $1B more. Rule 6: at most one new launch per round
tests.numbers:
- NGSA development ran 2030-37. A350 Re-engine development would run 2045-50, with EIS in 2050.
- Overlap: 0 years. Strain: $0. One launch this round, so rule 6 is met. The default also has 0 overlap.
- Against the NGSA ramp: NGSA reaches 1,194 in 2045 (99.5 a month) and 1,200 from 2046-47, so the ramp is essentially complete when Re-engine spend starts ($1.0B a year, 2045-49).
- The Re-engine is widebody and takes no narrowbody slots. Its engine chain (Trent XWB, UltraFan WB) is separate from CFM and the Joint Venture.
- Shared constraint: skilled engineering and industrial talent binds both rate and new programmes. That matters only if a step beyond 100 a month runs at the same time (see that test). It does not fail this test.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit A350 work-package absorption (ask 3a)
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed. Game proxy: not in round 1 (2030); round 2 (2035) at the earliest
tests.numbers:
- Proxy: round 3 (2045) is a round after the earliest round the proxy allows and ten years after the company's 2033-35 window.
- On the record: silent. No bulletin or brief reports A350F or Spirit A350 status. The A350F entered its industrial phase in 2025, twenty years ago on the game clock. Widebody deliveries have been flat at 70 a year (41.2% share) from 2026 to 2044, and no widebody quality or supply event is reported.
- What the silence means: I cannot certify absorption 'shown complete on the record', which I asked for in round 2, and the board will never show it. Nor does the silence give me a concrete production constraint to fail it on. It passes on the proxy only.

tests.name: Ramp shield (A320 and NGSA)
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with an open ramp commitment
tests.numbers:
- No A320 ramp commitment is open: the end-2027 date is long past, and the Alt plan runs down to 25 A320 in 2045 and none from 2047.
- The NGSA ramp reaches 100 a month by 2045-47.
- The Re-engine's $1.0B a year over 2045-49 buys widebody work and takes no narrowbody slots, engines or wing capacity.
- The test passes for both the default and the Re-engine.

tests.name: Engine readiness for the Re-engine on the board (teams.md Step 3)
tests.threshold: The Re-engine's engine (Rolls-Royce by default) adds 0 years to EIS on the grid
tests.numbers: On the board, the A350 Re-engine enters service 5 years after launch whatever the engine: 2050 for a 2045 launch. The grid ($5B at EIS, item +0.90 / +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.89 / -0.50 / -0.50) prices no engine gap. Because the engine never changes the grid, no $1B override could ever answer an engine objection. That is why I do not make it a veto ground.

tests.name: Widebody engine committed in time for the Re-engine (my round-2 2045-gate condition; ask 3c). Classification: supply flag, not a safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch test, and not a soft veto
tests.threshold: A widebody engine committed on the record and ready by the Re-engine's EIS (supply certainty)
tests.numbers:
- The A350 flies the Trent XWB today. No widebody engine for a Re-engine is launched.
- UltraFan WB is ready 6 years after its launch, against the Re-engine's 5. Rolls-Royce says: 'No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table.'
- If Rolls-Royce launches in this sealed round, UltraFan WB is ready in 2051, one year after the board's 2050 EIS. If it waits for our launch to go public in the 2050 bulletin, it is ready in 2056, six years late.
- The GEnx upgrade (ready since 2033) is a 787 engine. Nothing on the record makes it an A350 engine.
- So the board's 2050 date is not an operating date: the engine sets it.
- Would a public invitation resolve it? It is necessary but not sufficient. It puts a Re-engine on the table in Rolls-Royce's terms, but it is published with our order, so on the public rules it cannot bring an engine before 2051 and probably not before 2056.
- My round-2 condition (an engine committed a round ahead) cannot be met under Rolls-Royce's stated policy before we launch. On its own it is therefore no reason to hold forever.
- Result: not met. It is a supply flag and binds nothing.

tests.name: Quality and the five pillars (ask 7)
tests.threshold: No order or public line that contradicts safety, quality, integrity, compliance or security
tests.numbers:
- The default orders (ngsa hold, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt) contradict no pillar. `rea350: launch` on its own contradicts none either.
- Conditions on the public line:
  1. No widebody engine is promised before one is committed.
  2. No Re-engine EIS date. If tabled, give a window that follows the engine and is gated on durability, never 2050.
  3. No rate number beyond 100 a month, only a window.
  4. No reference to Delay Tactics.
  5. Describe NGSA engines accurately: CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, three makers and two sources.
  6. Retire last round's 'final phase of development' line, since NGSA is in service.

tests.name: Capacity beyond 100 a month (ask 4; unpriced other move)
tests.threshold: A disciplined and controlled step only once NGSA holds 100 a month on its KPIs with no open quality finding; both engine sources, the in-house wing and titanium and forgings are committed for our own extra volumes; and no supply crunch is reported
tests.numbers:
- Need: the waiting backlog grows 107 (2045), 223 (2047), 616 (2050), 1,384 (2053), 1,824 (2055) and 2,297 (2060). Delivered share is 63.7% against 80% preference from 2047.
- Supply today: 2,400 engines a year from 2047 across CFM and the Joint Venture. The record holds no measurement of CFM, Joint Venture, wing, titanium or forging capacity above that.
- CFM's public line: LEAP durability kits and deliveries come first, and it fixes the supply base before loading it. In 2025 the rate slipped on engines.
- My recommendation: prepare, do not commit. Open capacity talks with both engine sources for our own extra volumes only, with no exclusivity and nothing drawn from Boeing's LEAP-1B allocation (that would read as `bottleneck`). Size the in-house wing and the Aubert & Duval titanium and forgings first, and staff it from our own pipeline.
- No rate number in public, only a window.
- If the Re-engine is also launched, sequence the step so that the two do not run as concurrent new work without my supply test passing.

tests.name: Delay Tactics (rules 4 and 5, integrity pillar; ask 5)
tests.threshold: At most one move per game, only after fps is public and before its EIS; `both` counts as two moves; `poaching` only with an Airbus programme in development; `bottleneck` and `both` never (integrity)
tests.numbers:
- fps is not public, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine (rule 4).
- On the hold row, against the default: one move -11.45 / -0.18 / -0.18 / -0.21 / -0.18 / -11.46 / -0.19; both moves -11.71 / -0.37 / -0.37 / -0.42 / -0.37 / -11.72 / -0.38.
- On the Re-engine row, against the Re-engine: one move -11.47 / -0.19 / -0.19 / -0.21 / -0.19 / -11.47 / -0.20; both moves -11.73 / -0.38 / -0.38 / -0.43 / -0.38 / -11.73 / -0.39.
- No column gains, because our capacity binds.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037, so nothing is in development on the hold row and `poaching` also breaks rule 5.
- `bottleneck` and `both` breach integrity. My integrity verdict stands.

tests.name: Integrity and supply of the other moves (ask 6)
tests.threshold: Secure our own supply for our own ramp, never a claim on a rival's capacity; recruit from our own pipeline, never by targeting a rival's team
tests.numbers:
- Own supply: the in-house wing, the Aubert & Duval titanium and forgings, and the raw-materials watchlist, for our own ramp only.
- CFM agreements: our own NGSA volumes (and the A320neo tail to 2046), with no exclusivity and nothing above our ramp. If a step beyond 100 a month is studied, any added request is for our own volumes and never against Boeing's LEAP-1B allocation.
- Skills: apprenticeships, graduates and universities in Europe, with no targeted hiring.
- Widebody engine invitation, if tabled: open to every widebody maker on standard terms, with no exclusivity.
- All are ready for the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee review.

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If reported: re-time, never cancel
tests.numbers: None is reported. NGSA has been in service since 2037, and the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, CFM ducted since 2041 and CFM-Embraer since 2042.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: our own disciplined ramp
tests.numbers: The 2030-only option lapsed. The 737 holds 57 a month as a ceiling with KPI gates. None of our programmes changes.

vetoes.plan: Any Delay Tactics value (`bottleneck`, `poaching` or `both`), on the hold row or the Re-engine row
vetoes.ground:
Company red line, rule 4: fps is not public, so any move is naked and exposed to the $48.32B fine.
- `both` is two moves.
- `poaching` on the hold row also breaks rule 5, because nothing is in development.
- `bottleneck` and `both` breach the integrity pillar.
- Margin against the best passing option: one move is -11.45 / -11.46 in S1/S6 on the hold row (-11.47 on the Re-engine row) and -0.18 to -0.21 in the fps columns. Both moves are -11.71 / -11.72 (-11.73).
- A red line and a pillar, so no override is possible.

vetoes.plan: `rea350: launch` in 2045 (Alt plan, no Delay Tactics)

ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived (Very low confidence). Nothing of mine is on record, so I apply company doctrine.

NGSA: in service since 2037, 1,194 aircraft in 2045, 100 a month from 2047. No quality finding, supply crunch or engine slip is reported. It stays on the Board's twice-yearly product-safety review. Engines: CFM plus the Joint Venture, 2 sources and 3 makers in 2045 and 2050. The record holds no durability or life-limited-part data on the Joint Venture engine. P&W's own terms put GTF2's tested configuration in service first; CFM stays the backstop.

A350 Re-engine: it passes my safety, quality, ramp-shield, supply-crunch, capacity and absorption tests. Zero overlap, $0 strain, one launch. Absorption passes on the proxy only; the record is silent.

The engine is a supply flag, not a veto. UltraFan WB needs six years, and Rolls-Royce waits for a Re-engine on the table. Launched in the same sealed round it is ready in 2051; after our launch is public, 2056. The board says 2050; the engine sets the real date. An invitation is necessary, not sufficient. My round-2 condition cannot be met before a launch, so it is no reason to hold forever.

I recommend hold: no engine, and no $1B. If you table it, I concur, provided we invite engine proposals on standard terms, prove durability before entry into service, and give a window that follows the engine, never 2050.

Beyond 100 a month: prepare, do not commit. Engines set the rate.

Binding: any Delay Tactics.

other_moves.move: Secure our own supply for NGSA at rate
other_moves.detail:
This continues the round-1 and round-2 programme, now for NGSA in steady production.
- The NGSA wing stays in-house.
- Aerostructures come through Airbus Atlantic, Airbus Aerostructures and the ex-Spirit sites.
- Titanium and forgings come through the Aubert & Duval co-ownership and additive (DED) parts.
- The critical raw-materials and rare-earths watchlist continues.
It serves our own production only and makes no claim on any rival's capacity [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

other_moves.move: NGSA engine supply: CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, at our own volumes
other_moves.detail:
NGSA is fitted with CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine. That is two sources from three engine makers.
- The capacity agreements with both cover only our own NGSA volumes (and the A320neo tail), with no exclusivity and nothing above our own production.
- The aim is supply certainty, not leverage [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s, and its production ramp-up is now reaching its planned rate. We will continue a disciplined and controlled ramp-up: every step is gated on safety, on quality and on the readiness of our supply chain, and safety and quality come before schedule. Our customers have a choice of engine, from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, and our supply agreements are matched to our own volumes. The A320neo family is completing an orderly transition to the new aircraft. Demand for the new aircraft remains strong. With our suppliers we are preparing the next step in our industrial capacity, and we will take it when our safety, quality and supply indicators say so, not before. On widebodies, our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F, which we continue to improve for our customers. We continue to secure key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. The new aircraft was funded from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: the company default on every lever, on our own clock.
- Orders: `ngsa: hold` (in service since 2037, engine code fixed), `rea350: hold`, `delay_tactics: none`, `a320_plan: alt`.
- Every field is at its default, so there are no Board items and no override. The game's single override stays unspent.
- The A350 Re-engine was genuinely considered at the 2045 gate and is not tabled. The tests that stopped it are named below and in `board_response`.

THE ROUND AGAINST MY PAID OBJECTIVES, IN ORDER
1. Five pillars: no order or line contradicts them (Wagner, ask 7). No safety, quality, supply-crunch or engine-slip event is on the record [AX-0073, AX-0081].
2. Ramp: NGSA delivers 1,194 aircraft in 2045 and 1,200 a year (100 a month) from 2047, and the Alt plan runs out by 2047. Our own factory ceiling, not preference, now binds. That is why I prepare a capacity step on Wagner's gates and do not commit it.
3. Airbus of the 2030s and beyond: NGSA entered service in 2037, two years after the technology-ready year, with no slip. The widebody question is the one strategic lever left. It does not clear our own launch bar this round.
4. Board: the default is never vetoed. A Re-engine tabled against an unresolved ExCo soft veto would be vetoed.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
Deleted as red lines or pillars (never traded for PV):
- Every Delay Tactics row. Under rule 4 fps is not public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
- One move on the hold row is -11.45 / -0.18 / -0.18 / -0.21 / -0.18 / -11.46 / -0.19; both moves are -11.71 to -11.72 in S1/S6. It gains in no column, even where fps launches, because our 1,200-a-year capacity binds.
- `both` is two moves. `bottleneck` and `both` fail integrity. `poaching` on the hold row breaks rule 5.
- The team's stricter condition stays in force: I record no set-aside.

Tested:
- Default: passes every Toepfer test (peak cash $0.0B against $5.2B; worst S7 +12.78; net cash rebuilt) and every Wagner test.
- `rea350: launch`:
  - passes peak cash ($1.0B a year, $4.2B headroom), overlap and rule 6 (0 years, $0 strain, one launch), and the teams.md robustness form (worst S7 +12.28);
  - passes all of Wagner's safety, quality, ramp-shield, supply-crunch, capacity and absorption tests, with a non-binding engine-supply flag;
  - FAILS Toepfer's robustness test as he applied it in round 2 and again now: the item is +0.90 / +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.89 / -0.50 / -0.50, negative in plausible columns S6/S7 and short of $1B in every column and on every weighting. He marks it binding.
- I accept his test as well founded. His stricter reading goes beyond the teams.md form, but it is the company's own A350 Re-engine launch test (profile §6: at least $1B over Do Nothing, including strain), which fails in every column.

Survivor: the default only.

Doctrine check, which gives the same answer on its own:
- Even if Toepfer's test had passed, the Re-engine is within $1B of the default on every weighting: +0.69 on my refreshed weights, +0.75 on round-2 weights, +0.49 equal-weighted, +0.90 at best.
- So the doctrine-default rule takes the default.
- The tie-breaks favour hold as well: the later capex start (none against $1.0B a year from 2045) and fewer Board items (0 against 1 Qualified Majority item).

Override:
- Not available, and not sought. The margin over the best passing option is +0.69 expected and +0.90 at best, under $1B.
- On a Qualified Majority item it is also behind in the worst column (-0.50).
- The Board would veto a Re-engine carried by an override or tabled against an unresolved objection. I hold no override against the Board.

WHAT HOLD COSTS, SAID PLAINLY
- About $0.69B on my weights against the best grid plan. The rule allows that cost, and it is not a premium.
- Nothing on the record prices a later launch (Toepfer, ask 6).
- A 787 Re-engine on the record would close it under rule 3, so holding now probably means no A350 Re-engine in this game. I accept that.
- The derivatives-first instinct [AX-0082] argued for it. But a launch with no widebody engine committed, a company bar unmet in every column and a binding CFO test is not a disciplined launch.
- Wagner's engine flag is real but not decisive. UltraFan WB would be ready in 2051 at the earliest against the board's 2050 entry into service, and in 2056 if Rolls-Royce waits for our launch to be public. Supply certainty is the test I apply to every target [AX-0054].

SCENARIO TABLE (weight; default row; Re-engine row, not tabled)
- S1, Boeing holds (modal), 40%: +13.71; +14.61
- S2, 10-year fps, 25%: +12.88; +13.77
- S3, 10-year fps at Renton, 5%: +12.88; +13.77
- S4, 7-year fps, 5%: +12.88; +13.77
- S5, fps via Embraer, 10%: +12.88; +13.77
- S6, 787 Re-engine, 10%: +13.61; +13.11
- S7, 10-year fps + 787 Re-engine, 5%: +12.78; +12.28
Weighted, the default is +13.28 (+13.20 on round-2 weights, +13.09 equal) and the Re-engine row +13.97. The worst plausible column is S7 on both rows. The item stays positive in expectation unless S6 and S7 together exceed about 64%.

BOARD GATE
No Board items. For the record, the default row:
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: pass (peak cash, robustness, net cash, no raise or cut).
- Wagner: pass (ramp, quality, engines, no crunch).
- Grid ΔPV: +13.71 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +13.61 / +12.78.

Not tabled, `rea350: launch` (Qualified Majority, $5B):
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: peak cash pass ($1.0B a year, $4.2B headroom); robustness FAIL, a binding soft veto.
- Wagner: pass, with a non-binding engine-supply flag.
- Item ΔPV against hold: +0.90 / +0.89 x4 / -0.50 / -0.50.
- Stopped by Toepfer's robustness test and the company's $1B launch test.

FLAGS I CARRY
- Joint Venture engine durability and full-life parts: a watch item on the product-safety review, with CFM as the backstop.
- The capacity step beyond today's rate: prepared, not committed. Its capex needs its own cash line.
- Waiting backlog: 616 in 2050 and 2,297 in 2060. Delivered share is 63.7% against 80% preference.
- Rule 3: watch for any 787 Re-engine on the record.

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Here's what we know. Our new CFM engine, a step forward from today's LEAP, has been ready since 2041, and it's on Airbus's new single-aisle. We're working with Embraer, together with Safran, so that engine has a home on more than one airframe. We thank our customers for that.

We hold that engine to the standard our customers set and we set for ourselves: durability proven before entry into service, hot and harsh conditions included. Test and field data go to our customers and our Board first. They don't go into a press line.

We're not launching anything new this year. RISE stays our technology programme with Safran. Testing goes on, and what we learn keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet. We won't put a date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it.

LEAP durability kits and deliveries still come first. On capacity, we work with both airframers, together with Safran.

Boeing has invited us to bring a proposal for its next single-aisle. Together with Safran, we've answered on product, and we'll be at the table. We don't have a birthright on that order. When and what Boeing launches is Boeing's call.

Here's what we don't know: when that airplane launches, and what it flies with. When we know, you'll know. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW DO WE WIN [CX-0467]
For this board, the launch game is over.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 on code 7, and its code can no longer change.
- Our Ducted has been ready since 2041, Partner Embraer has counted since 2042, and the GEnx upgrade since 2042.
- The P&W-RR Joint Venture is formed, with its engine ready since 2036.
- The one launch on the menu is an Open Fan into an 18-year airframer wait, and Lobby only works with it.
So the game is the installed base we hold: the 737 slot, our share of NGSA, the A320neo and the GEnx [CX-0422]. We win it by proving what we launched in test and in the field, keeping kits and deliveries first, and earning our seat on Boeing's next single-aisle with a durability record behind it. We don't have a birthright on that order [CX-0564]. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

DECISION
Hold everything: ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions and genx all on hold (option A, Do Nothing).
- Ghai and Ali each recommended it on their own.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- No colleague's binding test fails, so there are no overrides.

THE TESTS
1. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609].
- Hold is the best row in both columns: -24.29 (S1) and -22.48 (S2).
- Open Fan + Lobby against hold: -16.73 / -16.74 on a $9B bill.
- Open Fan alone: -18.96 / -18.97 on $8B.
- Each Open Fan plan loses more than its bill in every column: that is the wait penalty behind NGSA's 2037 entry. Lobby is +2.23 on the Open Fan, but only on a base that fails.
- Lobby alone is about -1.00 a column. That's an inference from the rules: the flat $2B strain is already in the hold row, and Lobby does nothing alone.

2. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536].
- Expected column: S1, the record. Weights: S1 75 / S2 25.
- Weighted hold is -23.84 (-24.11 at 90/10, -23.93 at 80/20, -23.38 at 50/50). Hold is best at every weight, so the weights set the booking, not the choice.
- I book -24.3, on S1. S2's +1.81 gets credit only when a Boeing fps is on the record.

3. The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469].
- An Open Fan launched in 2045 is ready in 2055, 18 years after NGSA's entry. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060.
- Ali confirms that S2's 2055 fps entry doesn't help: the first new narrowbody sets the wait.
- The RISE allowance can't carry it: the cheapest plan costs $16.73B (S1) and $16.74B (S2) against hold, above $15B.
- So no Open Fan launch. RISE stays whole as technology with no cancel (H5) [CX-0174, CX-0398]. That's the seed corn [CX-0256], and it becomes a product when an airframer wants it.

4. Ducted only as a defence (H3).
- Not in play: ducted is hold-only, already ready, and can't be cancelled.
- It is never called the next generation. The statement says 'a step forward from today's LEAP'.

5. Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]?
- Hold adds no project and no strain.
- Ali still can't show the floor margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites. That's the third time. It's advice, not a veto, and I own the gap with him.
- Doctrine applies: lean before capital, kits first, any new load gated on floor data, and LEAP-1B built to deliveries.

6. The next generation: my 20% line [CX-0217].
- It doesn't arise, because no Open Fan is ordered. RISE stays the 20%-or-better engine.
- Durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208]. Ali confirms hold trades nothing.

7. Tie-break: not needed. The gap to the next plan is $16.73B, far outside ε.

8. Premium: $0. Game total: $0 of $4.0B. The RISE allowance is unused.

THE JOINT VENTURE MISS
In 2035 I predicted no Joint Venture, and it formed.
- The package's S1 row was -21.53; the record is now -24.29.
- R&D and strain are unchanged at $6.0B, so the whole $2.76B is engine value. Ghai checked it, and I read it as the Joint Venture's cost to us (inference).
- The lesson: orders are simultaneous. A rival's condition that it can meet itself in the same round ('we commit when our partner does'), at no new spend, is a live column, not a no.
- Applied here, I move Boeing's fps from my frame's 20% to Ghai's 25%. Boeing's conditions are its own to meet, and 2045 is the last round in which a 10-year fps counts inside the NB horizon. But a launch isn't free to Boeing the way P&W's commitment was free to P&W, and Boeing has said 'not yet' twice. So I stop at 25.

SAFRAN GATE (H7, the CFM parity rule)
- No CFM narrowbody order this round.
- An Open Fan into a wait is outside joint practice, and I have no reason to give why Safran would agree, so it's not ordered. Neither is Lobby, which serves only that.
- The Boeing reply, the LEAP-1B allocation, Airbus's capacity agreements and the Embraer terms all go through CFM with Safran: product and supply only, no price or number before Safran agrees [CX-0184, CX-0160].
- RISE continues as technology with Safran, which is joint practice.
- GEnx is GE alone, and on hold.

THE BOARD'S CONDITIONS
- Ali raises no safety or durability flag.
- The three evidence gaps are named, with owners:
  - the Ducted's hot-and-harsh, dust and field data;
  - the LEAP-1B kit outcome;
  - RISE after October 2025.
  Absence of failure isn't clearance [CX-0009, CX-0012].
- 2041 held on the public record (ready since 2041 = launch + 6), so there is no re-price.
- No override, no premium, no Board item.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE
- the S2 weight (no precedent);
- the supply gating (Ali's floor record ends in 2025);
- the Embraer terms (Embraer isn't in my record).

BIAS CHECK
The installed-base lens could argue for launching RISE 'to seed the next 30 years' [CX-0555]. On this board it buys nothing: the wait penalty shows in every column. The low booking holds: last round I booked -26.3, and the record came in at -24.29. We raise to the record and no further.

WHAT CHANGES MY MIND
- A test or field event on the Ducted, LEAP or RISE. The statement and the Boeing offer change, and the value booked from 2041 is re-priced if the date moved.
- A Boeing fps on the record. I re-weight and credit S2.
- A Boeing signal toward code 4, the Joint Venture alone. Only product answers that.
- A widebody Re-engine or rival widebody upgrade. I re-test the GEnx.
- An airframer path for RISE. None is possible on this board before 2056.
It ain't that hard [CX-0653].

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467]

The launch game is over for this board. NGSA has been in service since 2037 with all three makers fitted. Our Ducted has been ready since 2041, Partner Embraer has counted since 2042, and the GEnx upgrade has counted since 2042. The P&W-RR Joint Venture is on the record, with its engine ready since 2036. The one launch on the menu is an Open Fan into an 18-year airframer wait, and Lobby only works alongside it.

So the game is the installed base we already hold: the 737 slot, our third of NGSA, the A320neo, the GEnx. Our major economics happen in and around that base [CX-0422]. We win it three ways:
- proving in test and in the field that what we launched does what we said, on safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CX-0658];
- keeping LEAP kits and deliveries first;
- earning a seat on Boeing's next single-aisle with an engine that has a durability record behind it, when Boeing decides it's ready. We don't have a birthright on that order [CX-0564].

We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630]. On my reading this is a hold-everything round. The real work is in the other moves and in telling the Board and the market plainly what we know and what we don't [CX-0436]. That includes the fact that neither objective can be bought on this menu.

H1: never refuse an airframer, never lock one out. The Ducted is offered to both airframers, and Boeing's next single-aisle gets a CFM engine, a LEAP derivative at minimum [CX-0587, CX-0185].

H2: never press an airframer into the Open Fan wait. NGSA has been in service since 2037, and a 2045 Open Fan is ready in 2055, so no open_fan launch. The RISE allowance exception can't carry a $16.73B or larger cost with the wait in every column [CX-0205, CX-0469].

H5: never cancel RISE for cost while an airframer may want it. RISE stays funded as technology with Safran: no programme dividend, and no dial-down because there's no launch [CX-0174, CX-0398].

H7: the Safran gate on every CFM narrowbody order (open_fan, lobby_emissions) and on narrowbody price and capacity: Boeing's invitation, the LEAP-1B allocation, Airbus's capacity agreements and Embraer terms. No price or number before Safran agrees. GEnx is GE alone [CX-0184, CX-0160, CX-0166].

My line: a next-generation engine needs at least a 20% reduction in fuel burn [CX-0217]. It binds RISE, and it arises this round only if an Open Fan were ordered.

frame.initial_lean:
My lean, before the memos: hold everything. ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions and genx all on hold. That's option A.

Why:
- It's the grid's best plan in S1 (-24.29), in S2 (-22.48) and at every weighting.
- The only alternative is an Open Fan into an 18-year wait, which costs $16.73B or more against hold, beyond the cap and the allowance.
- No tie-break is needed: the gap is far outside my $1B ε.
- It isn't a Board item.

Weights S1 80 / S2 20. Expected column S1, the record. Book -24.3; S2 gets credit only when Boeing puts an fps on the record [CX-0248, CX-0536].

Premium $0; game total $0 of $4.0B; RISE allowance unused.

Bias check. The installed-base lens could tempt me to launch RISE "to seed the next 30 years" [CX-0555]. On this board it buys nothing: the wait penalty shows in every column. RISE stays the seed corn as technology [CX-0256], and becomes a product when an airframer wants it [CX-0469].

Objectives, said plainly:
- Open Fan: unmet and unreachable.
- NB share: unmet by 0.7 pp in 2045, with no order able to lift it.
We're not going for share [CX-0493], and I won't pay a premium that can't buy anything.

Other moves:
1. A product-only reply to Boeing's updated invitation, through CFM with Safran. We offer the Ducted with whatever durability record Mohamed's data supports, and a LEAP derivative as the floor. We accept proven durability before entry into service as our own standard. Any guarantee or time-on-wing term goes to Safran first.
2. Through CFM with Safran, on product and supply only, with no number before Safran agrees:
- the LEAP-1B allocation at 57 a month;
- Airbus's capacity agreements;
- Embraer terms.
3. RISE funded as technology with Safran.
4. LEAP kits and FLIGHT DECK first.
5. The cross-functional durability record on the Ducted.

Safran gate. No CFM narrowbody order this round. An Open Fan into a wait would be outside joint practice, and I couldn't give a reason Safran would agree.

Draft public line:
"Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. Here's what we know. Our new CFM engine, a step forward from LEAP, has been ready since 2041, and we're working with Embraer, with Safran. [Durability line only as Mohamed's evidence backs.] LEAP kits and deliveries still come first. We're not launching anything new this year. RISE stays our technology programme with Safran, with no date on it; it goes into service when an aircraft needs it. Together with Safran, we've answered Boeing's invitation on product, with durability proven before entry into service as our own standard. When and what Boeing launches is Boeing's call. Here's what we don't know: when that airplane launches. When we know, you'll know. It ain't that hard."

What changes my mind:
- A durability or quality flag from Mohamed: the statement and the Boeing offer change, though no order does.
- An airframer path for RISE on the record. None is in sight before 2056.
- Rahul showing a number that makes Lobby or the Open Fan pay. I don't expect one.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Things that would make me back an Open Fan or Lobby. Neither is in sight:
1. An airframer path for RISE on the record: a new narrowbody that isn't in service before the engine would be ready. On this board none is possible before 2056, since NGSA has been in service since 2037.
2. A grid row in which an Open Fan plan beats hold in the expected column, or loses no more than its bill in every column with the gap inside the $15B allowance.

Things that would raise the booking above -24.3:
1. A Boeing fps on the record. S2's +1.81 then becomes creditable, and I'd move to the weighted value.
2. Boeing deliveries back toward the 57-a-month ceiling.

Things that would lower it, booked the quarter we find them:
1. A Ducted durability or quality flag from Ali, or a slip from 2041. The value the grid books from 2041 gets re-priced. Dates and readiness are his ground.
2. A Boeing signal toward code 4.
3. 737 deliveries falling further below 458 a year.

Things that would change my weights:
1. A firm Boeing date, which raises S2 above 25.
2. A third 'not yet' from Boeing, which lowers it.

Things that would engage my terms veto: any price, concession or capacity number going to an airframer before Safran agrees.
cfo.memo:
Larry, your rows are right, and there's nothing to hide. Hold is -24.29 in S1 and -22.48 in S2: best in both columns and at every weight. The cheapest Open Fan plan costs $16.73B against hold, on a $9B bill, and still misses 2050: a 2045 launch is ready in 2055. That's above the $15B allowance and buys neither objective. My vetoes on any Open Fan and on Lobby alone stand. They're on the launch, not the R&D: RISE stays funded as technology.

The Joint Venture miss: R&D and strain are unchanged at $6.0B, so the whole $2.76B is engine value. We've been proven wrong on that one before. My lesson: a commitment that costs the rival nothing should be priced as live. Boeing's launch isn't free, but its conditions are its own to meet, and 2045 is the last round a 10-year fps counts. I'd put S2 at 25, not 20. It doesn't change the choice.

Book -24.3, the record. Credit S2's +1.81 only once Boeing puts an fps on the record.

Capital: $0 new spend against $2.55B of room. The Ducted came in at the $6.0B approved, no write-off. Payout whole, no rating risk.

Left out: a Boeing selection without us from 2055, a Ducted durability event, and 737 volume. Boeing delivered 458 aircraft in 2044 against 684 at 57 a month. Confirm the allocation as a ceiling, with Safran, and build to deliveries. But the good news is the installed base keeps paying.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (veto: dates): Open Fan launched in 2045, alone or with Lobby (options B and C; Culp's ask 1)
tests.threshold: Ready no earlier than launch + 10 and not before 2045. Any order whose value depends on an earlier ready year fails (inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times)
tests.numbers: A 2045 launch is ready in max(2045 + 10, 2045) = 2055. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060. The Open Fan rows (-43.25 S1 / -41.45 S2; with Lobby -41.02 / -39.22) book no gain before 2055. They carry only the wait penalty, which is set by NGSA's 2037 entry (-35 pp NB, or -20 pp with Lobby). No value rests on an earlier year, so the date passes. On ask 1, confirmed: 2055 is 18 years after NGSA's 2037 entry. S2's 2055 fps entry does not help, because the first new narrowbody sets the wait. To be ready by 2050, an Open Fan had to launch by 2040; the last round that allowed it was 2035 (ready 2045). Lobby takes effect immediately and has no ready year. Calc: /tmp/wargame-cfm/dash-2050-sd/work/r3_ali_calc.py.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (veto: dates): the hold row, i.e. Ducted, Partner Embraer and GEnx (Culp's ask 2: did 2041 hold?)
tests.threshold: Ducted ready no earlier than launch + 6. Partner Embraer counts 7 years after launch, on a CFM engine already ready. GEnx counts 3 years after launch, not before 2035, and on the widebody from 2042 if there is no Re-engine
tests.numbers: Ducted: 2035 + 6 = 2041. The public programme table reads 'ready since 2041', so on the board's record 2041 held and did not slip, and nothing triggers a re-price. Partner Embraer: 2035 + 7 = 2042, on a Ducted ready a year earlier. GEnx: 2030 + 3 = 2033. No widebody Re-engine is on the record, so it counts from 2042 (WB share 44.8% from 2042). The hold row (-24.29 / -22.48; -24.11 at 90/10, -23.93 at 80/20, -23.38 at 50/50) rests on 2041 and 2042 and no earlier year. 2041 comes from the board's development time. The test record behind it is not in our sources (see the safety-call test).

tests.name: Test, not analysis (veto: dates): Culp's draft public statement and other moves (Culp's ask 7, wording)
tests.threshold: Every date must be one a test can back: no ready year before launch plus development years; no RISE or Open Fan date of any kind (ready, fly demo, flight test, entry into service); no year by which a durability result is promised
tests.numbers:
- 'has been ready since 2041': 2035 + 6, on the public record. PASS.
- 'We're not launching anything new this year': no date. PASS.
- 'RISE ... with no date on it; it goes into service when an aircraft needs it': no demo, flight-test or entry year. PASS. My own fly demo slipped from 'by the middle of this decade' to 'this decade', so we promise none.
- Boeing reply, 'with durability proven before entry into service as our own standard': a test gate, not a year. PASS.
- 'When and what Boeing launches is Boeing's call': no year. PASS.
Condition on the bracket '[Durability line only as Mohamed's evidence backs]': our record holds no hot-and-harsh or dust result for the Ducted. The line can state the standard but not a result. The Board's suggested 'proven in test' would be a claim that no record in our hands backs (H6), so keep it out.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe (advice): Open Fan
tests.threshold: Ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry into service; otherwise the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby). Report the gap in years
tests.numbers:
Ready in 2055 against NGSA's 2037 entry: 18 years late in both S1 and S2. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060, 23 years late and after the NB count ends in 2056.
Item against hold:
- Open Fan: -18.96 (S1) / -18.97 (S2) on an $8B bill.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -16.73 / -16.74 on a $9B bill.
- Lobby on the Open Fan: +2.23 / +2.23.
H2 from the readiness side: hold, with RISE whole as technology.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe (advice): Ducted against Boeing's next single-aisle (Culp's ask 6, Boeing reply)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year, so a late date does not fail it
tests.numbers: Ready in 2041: 4 years after NGSA's 2037 entry (late, but earning from 2041). Against Boeing, it is 14 years before S2's 10-year fps entry (2045 + 10 = 2055) and 11 years before a 7-year fps (2052, off-grid). Boeing makes durability proven before entry into service a contract condition. 2041-2055 is a window for field data on NGSA, not a result. Whether durability is proven is a test result I do not have, and I will not answer it by analysis.

tests.name: Physics (advice): wording and Culp's 20% line (Culp's ask 7)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. Never call a ducted engine the next generation, since it has 'less than half' the open fan's gain
tests.numbers: Neither the brief nor the draft gives a fuel-burn figure. The Ducted is 'a step forward from LEAP' and never the next generation (H3, doctrine). RISE stays the engine of more than 20% fuel burn, SAF-ready and hydrogen-capable. 20% is 'practically impossible' without the open fan. Culp's 20% line arises only if an Open Fan is ordered, and I recommend none. Nothing trades durability for fuel burn.

tests.name: Durability first (advice)
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule (inference: Culp's line applied to my seat)
tests.numbers:
The frame makes durability claims, so the test applies. Hold trades nothing: no new programme, no new date, and LEAP kits and deliveries stay first.
Yardsticks for the Ducted:
- CFM56: about 17,000 cycles benign, 7,000-8,000 harsh.
- LEAP fleet leaders in 2023: 9,882 benign, about 4,800 harsh.
- Culp's kit targets: 8,000 harsh, 17,000 neutral.
The LEAP-1A kit (certified December 2024) more than doubles time on wing, matching the CFM56. It goes into every LEAP-1A delivery and is fitted at shop visits without adding visits. That is the durability record test and field data back. The Ducted's own numbers are not in our record, so none goes into the statement or the Boeing offer.

tests.name: Safety call (advice): the Board's evidence gaps and any flag (Culp's asks 2, 3 and 4)
tests.threshold: A problem that touches safety or durability goes to a cross-functional team, not one person. Say what we know, what we don't, and who owns each gap. Absence of failure is not clearance
tests.numbers:
(a) Ducted since 2041: no hot-and-harsh or dust turn-on/turn-off results and no NGSA test or field event are in our sources, which end in October 2025. The public record shows no event either: none in the 2045 bulletin, and Airbus's 2035 gate found no engine slip or quality event. That is absence, not clearance. Owner: me, with the joined supply-chain, engineering and quality team and Safran.
(b) LEAP-1B kit: certification with Boeing was due in 1H 2026, a year after my 2025 date. The outcome is not in our record. Boeing holds the 737 at 57 a month, asks to confirm the LEAP-1B allocation and names no durability event. It does list our concentrated sub-tier shortages as a watch item. Owner: me, with Boeing and the FAA.
(c) RISE after October 2025: the last items are 350+ tests with an early durability focus, 200+ hours of wind tunnel, HPT-blade dust testing from October 2025 and noise tests with Airbus. Nothing later is in our record, including the outcome of the ground and flight test planned 'this decade'. Owner: me, with Safran.
Flag: none, because no failure is in evidence. Any test or field event goes to the cross-functional team before any date, statement or offer moves.

tests.name: Supply load (advice, doctrine): stacking
tests.threshold: Two or more projects bring $2B of strain on the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain (inference; my supply role is in Culp's words only)
tests.numbers: Hold adds no project, no R&D and no strain; the flat $2B strain is already in the hold row. An Open Fan would put a fourth programme on the same supply base, alongside the Ducted, Partner Embraer and GEnx, for -18.96 / -18.97 against hold. The grid pays nothing for that load. Advise hold. This follows doctrine, not my record.

tests.name: Supply load (advice): floor margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites, and long-lead release (Culp's ask 5; the Board's ask in rounds 1 to 3)
tests.threshold: Floor evidence that the 9 suppliers at 15 sites behind 80% of shortages carry LEAP, the kits and the Ducted with margin, and that the Ducted's long-lead orders were released on floor data
tests.numbers:
Rate on the record: CFM delivered 2,592 NB engines a year in 2030-2036.
Load now, against that rate:
- 1,716 in 2045, 33.8% below;
- 1,605-1,716 in 2042-2045, 34-38% below;
- 2,016 a year from 2047, 22.2% below.
The 737 has delivered 409-468 aircraft a year since 2038. That is 818-936 LEAP-1B engines, 60-68% of the 1,368 a year that 57 a month would take. So we have shown output above today's load (inference: the board models airframe factories, not our suppliers), but that is not floor margin.
Our floor data ends in 2025 and comes in colleagues' words: 80% of shortages from 9 suppliers at 15 sites; material flow up more than 30% in Q3 2025; 550-600 engineers at supplier sites.
Long-lead release: the Ducted was ready on schedule in 2041, so its long-lead orders went out in time (inference). I cannot show they went out on floor data.
Through the NGSA ramp and the A320neo Alt plan, the record shows no engine slip. Airbus's Alt steps are a ceiling at or below today's rate, with NGSA first.
Owner: me. There is no evidence of how I run the floor: following doctrine, lean before capital and kits first.

tests.name: Supply load (advice): capacity and customers through CFM with Safran (Culp's ask 6)
tests.threshold: Requested volumes stay within what the record shows delivered; product and supply only; no number before Safran agrees
tests.numbers:
LEAP-1B at 57 a month is 1,368 engines a year, the rate CFM delivered for the 737 in 2030-2036. Since 2038 the 737 has taken 818-936 a year, so the allocation is a ceiling carried with room.
Airbus's capacity agreements: Airbus's own 2035 move states their scope (its A320neo and NGSA volumes from 2035, no exclusivity, nothing above its own ramp). That sits inside the 2,592 a year we delivered.
Whether each was signed through CFM with Safran is not in our record. It is commercial: no evidence, following Culp and Ghai.
Boeing reply: we can stand behind the LEAP-1A kit record and the test gate, not a record for the Ducted. Any time-on-wing guarantee goes to Safran first and is Ghai's ground.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign (advice)
tests.threshold: Widebody: prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture. Narrowbody: keep RISE technology flowing into LEAP while RISE matures; this does not argue against the Open Fan
tests.numbers: GEnx: the 2030 upgrade on a proven architecture is live and counts +5 pp WB from 2042 (44.8% WB share), with no new engine. No widebody Re-engine or rival widebody upgrade is on the record, so nothing triggers a re-test. Narrowbody: RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP, and RISE is not cancelled (H5).

vetoes.plan: Any public statement, Boeing sourcing reply, capacity answer or other move that gives a RISE or Open Fan date (ready, fly demo, flight test or entry into service), a Ducted ready year before 2041, or a year by which the Ducted's durability will be 'proven'. Culp's draft passes. This is recorded so the wording holds.
vetoes.ground: Dates not backed by real testing, binding ground 2: a date that no test backs. 2041 is 2035 + 6, on the public record, and may be stated. RISE has no test record in our hands after October 2025, and my own fly demo slipped from mid-decade to 'this decade', so it gets no date of any kind. The Ducted's hot-and-harsh and dust results are not in our sources, so no year can be put on 'proven'. Note: my veto right over programme dates is an inference. My own words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern believing durability-fix results. The team rule makes the veto bind unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch, alone or with lobby_emissions (options B and C)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a date veto: the 2055 date (launch + 10) passes. Readiness fails. The engine would be ready 18 years after NGSA's 2037 entry in every column; a 2050 launch would be ready in 2060. Item against hold: -18.96 / -18.97 on its own, and -16.73 / -16.74 with Lobby. Hold, and keep RISE whole as technology with Safran. Never cancel it: we failed twice, and we got it done.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch without an Open Fan (option D)
vetoes.ground: Advice. It raises no date issue, because it takes effect immediately. It buys nothing on the board without a live Open Fan. On whether to lobby I have no evidence: following Culp and Ghai. The technical facts I can supply: RISE is designed SAF-ready and hydrogen-capable, and noise tests with Airbus showed the open fan can be quieter than today's LEAP.

vetoes.plan: Durability wording in the public statement and the Boeing reply: any Ducted durability result, record or 'proven in test' claim
vetoes.ground: Advice; this is Culp's own H6 and durability line, not my date veto. Our sources hold no hot-and-harsh or dust turn-on/turn-off result for the Ducted, and no NGSA field data. The statement and the offer may state the standard (proven before entry into service, as Boeing's contract condition and our own) and the LEAP-1A kit record (certified December 2024, in every delivery, time on wing more than doubled). They may not state a Ducted result. If a Ducted durability claim appears in the decision, I will mark it as an H6 red-line breach in my veto check.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Test or field data only, never analysis.
(1) A hot-and-harsh or dust test result on the Ducted, or an NGSA field event, showing durability short of the standard. I would raise a flag and send it to the cross-functional team with Safran. The Boeing offer and the statement would change. If the in-service date had moved later than 2041, Culp would re-price the value the grid books from 2041. No order changes, because ducted is hold only.
(2) A LEAP-1B kit outcome showing the fix did not turn the problem off. I would flag it with Boeing and the FAA, and LEAP kits would stay ahead of everything else.
(3) RISE results from Safran showing a durability or dust problem. RISE stays technology either way, with no date.
(4) An airframer path for RISE on the record: no new narrowbody entering service before an Open Fan's ready year. Nothing on this board moves 2055 earlier, and NGSA's 2037 entry is fixed, so readiness keeps failing.
(5) Floor data at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites showing no margin for LEAP and the kits. I would then advise gating every new load, and the LEAP rate would come first.
ops.memo:
Turn on, turn off. I recomputed every date.

Open Fan launched now: ready 2055, launch plus ten. NGSA has flown since 2037, so that is eighteen years late. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060. The date passes and readiness fails. No test brings the objective back. Hold. RISE stays whole with Safran. We failed twice. We got it done.

Hold row: Ducted 2041, launch plus six. Embraer and GEnx count from 2042. Nothing rests on an earlier year. No veto.

Now what we promised and I can't yet show. Last round we said we'd prove the Ducted's durability, hot and harsh included, before service. The record says ready since 2041. The hot-and-harsh and dust results are not in the sources I have. Nor is the LEAP-1B kit outcome, due in the first half of 2026, or RISE after October 2025. No event is on the record either, but absence of failure is not clearance. I own all three, with the cross-functional team, Boeing, the FAA and Safran. No single person can make a safety decision.

So the statement says "ready since 2041" and claims no durability result. The Boeing offer carries our standard, proven before entry into service, not a record we can't show. What we can show is the LEAP-1A kit: certified, in every delivery, time on wing more than doubled.

Supply: we delivered 2,592 engines a year and carry 1,716. The margin at the nine suppliers is still not shown. Third time. I own it.

other_moves.move: Product-only reply to Boeing's updated sourcing invitation for its next single-aisle, through CFM with Safran
other_moves.detail: We offer the new CFM engine (the Ducted, ready since 2041), with a LEAP derivative as the floor (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. We accept durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition; it's our own standard. We stand behind what test and field data back: the LEAP-1A kit, certified in December 2024, in every LEAP-1A delivery, more than doubling time on wing [CX-0209, CX-0225]. The Ducted's hot-and-harsh and dust results go to Boeing only as the cross-functional team releases them, and we make no Ducted durability claim before then (Ali, H6). No price, no concession, no number. Any guarantee, time-on-wing commitment or penalty goes to Safran first and is modelled conservatively [CX-0184, CX-0979]. No ready year earlier than 2041, and no year by which durability will be 'proven'.

other_moves.move: Confirm Boeing's LEAP-1B allocation at today's rate (57 a month) as a ceiling for supply certainty, through CFM with Safran
other_moves.detail: Confirmed only once Safran agrees, with no price in it [CX-0184, CX-0160]. It's a backlog we share [CX-0197], and we won't get ahead of Boeing or the FAA on any rate step [CX-0307]. We plan to deliveries, not to the ceiling: the 737 took 818-936 LEAP-1B engines a year since 2038, 60-68% of the 1,368 a year that 57 a month would take. That's lean before capital, and it means no overcapitalisation (Ghai) [CX-0540].

other_moves.move: Airbus long-term capacity agreements (A320neo and NGSA, from 2035): confirm status and close any open item through CFM with Safran
other_moves.detail: Product and supply only, on standard terms. Any price term is a joint decision, with no number before Safran agrees [CX-0184]. Scope as Airbus states it publicly: its own A320neo and NGSA volumes, no exclusivity, nothing above its own ramp, with NGSA's first claim respected. Whether the agreements are signed is not on our record. Ghai reports the signature status to the Board.

other_moves.move: Partner Embraer: terms worked through CFM with Safran
other_moves.detail: No Embraer number goes to the market or to an airframer until terms are agreed with Safran (Ghai's condition) [CX-0184].

other_moves.move: Close the three durability evidence gaps cross-functionally and report them to the Board
Supplier-floor margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of shortages, reported to the Board before any new load
other_moves.detail: This is the third time the Board has asked, and it's still not met. I own it with Ali. We show the floor margin for LEAP, the kits and the Ducted together, and any new programme load is gated on that data. Kits and the LEAP rate come first. We build LEAP-1B to deliveries, not to the ceiling. This follows doctrine (lean before capital), because Ali's floor record ends in 2025 [CX-0613, CX-0540, CX-0653].

other_moves.move: Report the Ducted's 2035-2040 cash spend to the Board from the ledger
other_moves.detail: The board books $6.0B ($4.0B of R&D in 2035 plus $2.0B of strain) against $6.0B approved, with no overrun and no write-off. The yearly cash curve isn't in our brief, so Ghai reports it from the ledger against the $1.0B a year approved and the 2-3% band.

other_moves.move: RISE stays funded as a technology programme with Safran: ground, durability and dust testing continue; no product launch and no entry-into-service date
other_moves.detail: H5: no cancel and no programme dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398]. RISE becomes a product when an airframer wants it [CX-0469, CX-0205]. Continuing it as technology with Safran is joint practice. RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP [CX-0162]. The one RISE allowance stays unused.

other_moves.move: LEAP durability kits and supply-base work (FLIGHT DECK) continue ahead of everything else
other_moves.detail: Safety, quality, delivery, cost [CX-0658]. We fix the supply base we have before we load it [CX-0613, CX-0540].

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Here's what we know. Our new CFM engine, a step forward from today's LEAP, has been ready since 2041, and it's on Airbus's new single-aisle. We're working with Embraer, together with Safran, so that engine has a home on more than one airframe. We thank our customers for that.

We hold that engine to the standard our customers set and we set for ourselves: durability proven before entry into service, hot and harsh conditions included. Test and field data go to our customers and our Board first. They don't go into a press line.

We're not launching anything new this year. RISE stays our technology programme with Safran. Testing goes on, and what we learn keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet. We won't put a date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it.

LEAP durability kits and deliveries still come first. On capacity, we work with both airframers, together with Safran.

Boeing has invited us to bring a proposal for its next single-aisle. Together with Safran, we've answered on product, and we'll be at the table. We don't have a birthright on that order. When and what Boeing launches is Boeing's call.

Here's what we don't know: when that airplane launches, and what it flies with. When we know, you'll know. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW DO WE WIN [CX-0467]
For this board, the launch game is over.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 on code 7, and its code can no longer change.
- Our Ducted has been ready since 2041, Partner Embraer has counted since 2042, and the GEnx upgrade since 2042.
- The P&W-RR Joint Venture is formed, with its engine ready since 2036.
- The one launch on the menu is an Open Fan into an 18-year airframer wait, and Lobby only works with it.
So the game is the installed base we hold: the 737 slot, our share of NGSA, the A320neo and the GEnx [CX-0422]. We win it by proving what we launched in test and in the field, keeping kits and deliveries first, and earning our seat on Boeing's next single-aisle with a durability record behind it. We don't have a birthright on that order [CX-0564]. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

DECISION
Hold everything: ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions and genx all on hold (option A, Do Nothing).
- Ghai and Ali each recommended it on their own.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- No colleague's binding test fails, so there are no overrides.

THE TESTS
1. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609].
- Hold is the best row in both columns: -24.29 (S1) and -22.48 (S2).
- Open Fan + Lobby against hold: -16.73 / -16.74 on a $9B bill.
- Open Fan alone: -18.96 / -18.97 on $8B.
- Each Open Fan plan loses more than its bill in every column: that is the wait penalty behind NGSA's 2037 entry. Lobby is +2.23 on the Open Fan, but only on a base that fails.
- Lobby alone is about -1.00 a column. That's an inference from the rules: the flat $2B strain is already in the hold row, and Lobby does nothing alone.

2. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536].
- Expected column: S1, the record. Weights: S1 75 / S2 25.
- Weighted hold is -23.84 (-24.11 at 90/10, -23.93 at 80/20, -23.38 at 50/50). Hold is best at every weight, so the weights set the booking, not the choice.
- I book -24.3, on S1. S2's +1.81 gets credit only when a Boeing fps is on the record.

3. The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469].
- An Open Fan launched in 2045 is ready in 2055, 18 years after NGSA's entry. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060.
- Ali confirms that S2's 2055 fps entry doesn't help: the first new narrowbody sets the wait.
- The RISE allowance can't carry it: the cheapest plan costs $16.73B (S1) and $16.74B (S2) against hold, above $15B.
- So no Open Fan launch. RISE stays whole as technology with no cancel (H5) [CX-0174, CX-0398]. That's the seed corn [CX-0256], and it becomes a product when an airframer wants it.

4. Ducted only as a defence (H3).
- Not in play: ducted is hold-only, already ready, and can't be cancelled.
- It is never called the next generation. The statement says 'a step forward from today's LEAP'.

5. Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]?
- Hold adds no project and no strain.
- Ali still can't show the floor margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites. That's the third time. It's advice, not a veto, and I own the gap with him.
- Doctrine applies: lean before capital, kits first, any new load gated on floor data, and LEAP-1B built to deliveries.

6. The next generation: my 20% line [CX-0217].
- It doesn't arise, because no Open Fan is ordered. RISE stays the 20%-or-better engine.
- Durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208]. Ali confirms hold trades nothing.

7. Tie-break: not needed. The gap to the next plan is $16.73B, far outside ε.

8. Premium: $0. Game total: $0 of $4.0B. The RISE allowance is unused.

THE JOINT VENTURE MISS
In 2035 I predicted no Joint Venture, and it formed.
- The package's S1 row was -21.53; the record is now -24.29.
- R&D and strain are unchanged at $6.0B, so the whole $2.76B is engine value. Ghai checked it, and I read it as the Joint Venture's cost to us (inference).
- The lesson: orders are simultaneous. A rival's condition that it can meet itself in the same round ('we commit when our partner does'), at no new spend, is a live column, not a no.

other_moves.detail:
The formed Joint Venture runs to the terms we published in 2035, restated with one change: the Finance routing comes out of the public text.
(1) The partners share risk and investment equally. Each designs, makes and supports its own modules end to end, and a joint integration and test team works the interfaces.
(2) P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence, no data access and no transfer [P-1233].
(3) A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share. It is never credited with P&W technology, and never with cash beyond equal shares.
(4) The engine in service is GTF2's tested configuration. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block, and it would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life.
Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions. No date is given for any block.

other_moves.move: Standing offer to Boeing's next single-aisle and to Airbus: the in-service Joint Venture engine, on standard terms, no launch-style discounts
other_moves.detail:
This answers Boeing's standing invitation to all three engine makers. We offer the Joint Venture engine, which has been ready since 2036, in the standard now in service. It is offered on standard commercial terms, with no launch discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100], and the same terms apply on NGSA.
- On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven, the contract condition Boeing has set.
- A newer block would be a new development with its own durability proof. None is promised.
- A rival's price, including CFM's new engine and its Embraer partnership, does not move the offer.
- Nothing is said on either airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062], and nothing is aimed at Boeing's timing either way.

other_moves.move: In-service durability report and the Rolls-Royce block gate to the Governance and Public Policy Committee
other_moves.detail:
Eddy brings the data as they exist, and says so plainly where they do not yet exist:
(a) time on wing against plan, split by operating environment;
(b) removal intervals against Block D and the Advantage;
(c) severe-environment and fleet-leader findings;
(d) every life-limited part's life against full life, with any life-limit reduction;
(e) configuration percentages, AOG count, shop-visit rate, turn times and the pacing parts, run daily and reported weekly.
If the data show a shortfall, the disclosure says so, and we contain the problem before any new commitment.

The Rolls-Royce block gate, held to the Advantage rule:
- Configuration control: a joint configuration board, with P&W sign-off on every interface to the gear and core.
- Spares: no intermix in shop visits until the block is certified and its own spares are stocked.
- Testing: at least Advantage-level testing (3x the base programme) at severe-environment conditions [PX-0084][PX-0128]. Time on wing must be no worse than the fitted standard, with interface load tests on our gear and core.
- Parts: full-life parts at entry into service.
- Supply and support: Rolls-Royce's parts capacity qualified before rate, and its support in place before entry into service.
The data go to the committee, and the block waits for its clearance. No date is given. If the data are late, the block waits.

other_moves.move: Annual whole-programme NPV review to the Finance Committee
other_moves.detail:
From Mitchill's memo.

(a) Booked figure: -0.14 = engine value +1.86 less R&D 2.00, charged undiscounted. 'Capitalise on the GTF' is reported as not met.

(b) The bridge from +0.48 (2035) is -0.62, all of it engine value. As PV at 2026:
- 2037-41: +0.11;
- 2042-44: -0.18 (936 engines against 976 in 2044);
- 2045-56: -0.56 (876 a year against 920).
Derived reading of the public tables, labelled inference: the fold and the equal-share rule cost nothing against the S1 path (our 2041 NGSA share of 38.4% matches the projection). From 2042, CFM's ducted engine and its Embraer partnership took about 3.9 pp of NGSA, half of it from us. That is about 44 engines a year.

(c) The end-state share of 23.3% is derived as 876 engines out of 3,768 NB engines (NGSA at 100 a month plus the MAX at 57, all CFM). Against the 2035 S4 projection (+2.63) the gap is -2.77. The +2.15 that S4 projected never showed: 2041 came in at exactly the S1 figure.

(d) S2 sits -0.59 below S1. A Boeing fps puts NGSA under the two-airframe share rule while the MAX stays on CFM, and the fps's P&W slot enters service only in 2055, against an NB count that ends in 2056. The brief has no S2 year table, so the gap cannot be placed by year.

(e) Comparisons:
- Against a buyback (PV 0): -0.14, not met.
- Against Do Nothing: no row in this brief. The direction only: from 2046 all 876 engines a year fly on NGSA.
- Derived return with R&D discounted at 10% (ratable $0.33B a year over 2030-35): about +0.77, with a range of +0.49 to +1.01. Labelled derived, for Finance only, never booked and never public.

other_moves.move: Enterprise risk register update to the Audit Committee and the full Board
other_moves.detail:
Retire the 2035 risk that Airbus moves NGSA to code 5. It is moot: NGSA is in service with P&W fitted.

Add three risks:
(1) In-service durability and time on wing of the NGSA engine. It now holds the credibility objective, and no fleet data are yet in the brief.
(2) Share pressure from CFM's ducted engine and its Embraer partnership.
(3) Joint Venture alignment with Rolls-Royce: its 'own test programme' for the folded UltraFan and its separate UltraFan offer to Boeing.

Watch item: gear-and-core pacing parts sized to the whole Joint Venture flow (about 1,750 modules a year, derived) and to the GTF shop base (about 12,100 engines since 2026, derived).

other_moves.move: Written alignment confirmation sought from Rolls-Royce; any cash or block cost to Finance as a capital item
other_moves.detail:
We ask Rolls-Royce to confirm in writing two things. First, that UltraFan content enters only as a later block on the Joint Venture engine, through the joint team and our gate. Second, that any Boeing offer it makes is the Joint Venture engine.

A block that brings its own gear or core is not a block on our engine. It would be the alignment break, and a Board-level risk [P-1875].

Any Rolls-Royce request for a technology credit in cash beyond equal shares, any block integration cost beyond equal shares, and any fleet-cost overrun return to Finance as a capital item. Mitchill would veto the first on ground 3. This routing stays in the private record.
