pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Bad news first. The new single-aisle market is more contested than when we committed. CFM's new engine has been ready since 2041, and CFM has a partnership with Embraer. We have no birthright on any aircraft, and we earn our place every day. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. The fleet work goes on. The Hot Section durability upgrade is offered to GTF operators through our MRO network, and fleet spares come ahead of new hardware.

We control what we can control. The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, built on GTF2's tested configuration, has been ready since 2036. It is fitted on Airbus's new single-aisle, which has been in service since 2037. Time on wing is the name of the game. We will report that engine's durability as the in-service data show it, and not ahead of them. We are sizing parts, spares and shop capacity to the fleet we support, the GTF and the new engine together.

The Joint Venture shares risk and investment equally. It never shares our core technology. Pratt & Whitney designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules, under its own type data. A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share, never through ours. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block. It would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions.

Our engine is on offer to any new single-aisle, Boeing's included, on standard terms, with no launch discounts. On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates.

The dividend comes first. This year's plan needs no new engine development spending and no change to the dividend or to our path on debt.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo hold; jv_with_rr hold. Both are the only legal values (brief section 3), and both are the default, so nothing goes to the Board. premium_b is 0 and overrides is empty.

THE TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP:

(1) Start from Eddy's proposal. He proposes hold and hold, and Mitchill recommends the same.

(2) Strike any plan that fails a binding veto. None does.
- Mitchill: ground 1 (dividend and debt) is not engaged at $0 of new R&D. Ground 2 (unselected engine) is not applicable, because no live GTF2 exists and the Joint Venture engine is selected and fitted on NGSA. Ground 3 (terms) passes. Ground 4 (upside) passes.
- Mitchill's two conditional vetoes, on a partner credit beyond equal shares and on overclaiming in the disclosure, are not engaged. I took his wording fixes into the statement: 'no new engine development spending'; 'CFM's new engine has been ready since 2041'; 'any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block'.
- Eddy: both grounds pass. The engine has been ready since 2036, against NGSA's 2037 and S2's 2055, and no block, date or durability claim appears. His watch item is not triggered. I took his edits: 'Under the Joint Venture's terms'; 'sizing', not 'sized'.

(3) Safety and durability set the constraint [PX-0035][PX-0073]. No Rolls-Royce block enters service before its own proof and full-life parts reach the Governance and Public Policy Committee, and GTF2's tested configuration stays the fitted standard until then. Eddy has no fleet data to show, so the disclosure claims no durability for the NGSA engine. It says we will report it as the data show it.

(4) Optimise. There is one row: 'GTF2: hold', -0.14 (S1) / -0.73 (S2). It is the best grid plan in both columns because it is the only one.

(5) Tie-breaks. 'The fleet beats a new engine' governs the other moves. 'Miss a cycle' does not apply: the Joint Venture engine is already ready for any code that includes us, and S2 is code 7. A rival's discount moves nothing.

WEIGHTS: S1 0.60, S2 0.40. I move from my framing 0.65/0.35 to Mitchill's and the Board's 0.40.
- For S2: Boeing's NB delivery share fell from 40.1% to 26.6%, its balance sheet is repaired, and its sourcing move names code 7. Those are lead indicators.
- My own incrementalism on a rival's timing [PX-0093] pulls me low, and Mitchill books downside early.
- Expected PV: 0.6 x -0.14 + 0.4 x -0.73 = -0.376, reported as -0.38. Worst column: S2, -0.73.
- The row is negative at any weights, and nothing on the orders turns on them.
- I say nothing on Boeing's dates [PX-0062], and nothing we do is aimed at its timing either way.

THE HONEST ACCOUNT (Mitchill's numbers; I trust his cash over my dates):
- The booked -0.14 is engine value +1.86 less R&D 2.00, charged undiscounted.
- The -0.62 since 2035 is all engine value, a step, not timing. Through 2041 we ran at or above plan. From 2042, CFM's ducted engine and its Embraer partnership took about 3.9 pp of NGSA, half from us. That is about 44 engines a year: 920 became 876. The attribution is derived inference from public tables.
- Our 2035 grid had no CFM column. The +2.15 that S4 projected never showed.
- S2 is -0.59 below S1 because the two-airframe share rule cuts Airbus's preference while the MAX stays on CFM, and the fps's P&W slot enters service only in 2055, against an NB count that ends in 2056. The fps volume beyond 2056 is real in 'miss a cycle' terms [PX-0071], but it is RTX-wide in my record, inferred here, and not booked.
- The derived WACC-discounted figure (about +0.77) goes to Finance only. It is never booked and never public.

DISCLOSURE: the GTF2 'due ready 2036 ... carrying it through' lines are retired as history. 'Responsible bets with responsible paybacks' [PX-0010] is dropped, because -0.14 does not support it. The Boeing line is a condition, not a forecast. 'Never' is the public floor on technology credit, and the Finance routing moves to the private record. Counsel reviews the GTF paragraph.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD: my record is Low on the Rolls-Royce Joint Venture. Its governance, the block gate and the alignment request follow company doctrine [P-1233][P-1240][P-1875], Eddy's seat doctrine and Mitchill's cash test. I defer to Eddy on readiness, parts and capacity.

BIASES WATCHED:
- Operating-date optimism: no block, ramp or recovery date is given.
- Architecture loyalty: GTF2's configuration stays the standard only until Rolls-Royce's proof is in, not as pride.
- Incrementalism on Boeing: I corrected toward Mitchill's 0.40.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighed heavily, as the team rule and my profile direct: I trust Mitchill's cash numbers over my own operating dates.
- Adopted: his weights (0.60/0.40), the expected PV of -0.38 and S2 as the worst column, the envelope check ($0 new R&D, GTF2's $2.0B covering our $2B share, no fold write-off), and the dividend and debt confirmation.
- His NPV bridge goes to the Finance Committee as written. The -0.62 is a step from CFM's moves from 2042, not timing. The S4 +2.15 never showed. The end-state 23.3% is derived.
- His candour that the 2035 grid had no CFM column, and that the low end was put in the wrong place, is the account I own.
- His explanation of S2 corrects mine on two points: Airbus's free slots, and the possibility that part of the gap sits in delivered years.
- His wording fixes are all taken, and his advice on term (3) is taken: 'never' stays public, the routing goes private.
- His two conditional vetoes (ground 3 on any partner credit beyond equal shares, ground 4 on any overclaim) are respected and not engaged.
- The derived +0.77 stays labelled, for Finance only.
- His 'fail' on the programme return against a buyback is reported, not hidden. No order can change it.
memo_weighing.ops:
Weighed as binding on readiness, durability and capacity, where I defer to him. His record rests on one event, June 2023 (Low), and he says items 5 to 7 are seat doctrine and inference.
- Adopted: his proposal (hold, hold) and his readiness check (ready 2036 against NGSA's 2037 and S2's 2055; no gap on the board).
- The most important line in either memo is his: the brief carries no fleet data, so we claim no durability for the NGSA engine. He will not say there is no surprise coming, having said that five weeks before the recall. That sets the disclosure.
- His derived point that every Joint Venture engine carries our gear and core, about 1,750 modules a year, goes into the fleet move and the risk register. That flow, not 876, is what the pacing parts must be sized to.
- His Rolls-Royce block gate, held to the Advantage rule, goes to the Governance and Public Policy Committee as written.
- His alignment test (a block that brings its own gear or core is not a block on our engine) and his request for written confirmation from Rolls-Royce are taken as a private move.
- His three disclosure edits are taken.
- No veto is engaged. His watch item stands for any later block, date or durability claim.

'Bad news first. The new single-aisle market is more contested than when we committed. CFM has a new engine in service and a second airframe partner, and we earn our place on every aircraft, every day. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. The fleet work goes on: the Hot Section durability upgrade is offered to GTF operators through our MRO network, and fleet spares come ahead of new hardware.

We control what we can control. The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, built on GTF2's tested configuration, has been ready since 2036. It is fitted on Airbus's new single-aisle, in service since 2037. Time on wing is the name of the game. We will report that engine's durability as the in-service data show it, and we are sizing parts, spares and shop capacity to the fleet we support.

The Joint Venture shares risk and investment equally. It never shares our core technology: Pratt & Whitney designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules. Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block, and it will not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions.

Our engine is on offer to any new single-aisle, Boeing's included, on standard terms, with no launch discounts. On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates.

The dividend comes first. This year's plan needs no new development spending and no change to the dividend or to our path on debt.'

BIASES I AM WATCHING:
- Optimism on operating dates: no block, ramp or recovery date is given.
- Architecture loyalty: GTF2's configuration stays the standard only until Rolls-Royce's proof is in, not as a matter of pride.
- Incrementalism on Boeing's timing.

Through 2041 we ran at or above plan. From 2042, CFM's ducted engine and Embraer partnership took our NGSA share from about 38% to 36.5%: 44 engines a year to 2056. ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: gtf2_solo: hold; jv_with_rr: hold. These are the only legal values in the brief (section 3), so nothing goes to the Board.

gtf2_solo HOLD. GTF2 was launched in 2030 and was due ready in 2036. It folded into the Joint Venture in 2035, and its tested configuration is the engine fitted on NGSA. It can no longer be launched, cancelled or relaunched, and it needs no new R&D. Grid row 'GTF2: hold': -0.14 (S1) / -0.73 (S2). I take no view on the weights; that is Neil's.

jv_with_rr HOLD. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and the rules allow a withdraw only before formation, so my 2035 withdraw conditions have lapsed as orders. Both technical conditions still hold, as governance:
(1) the Joint Venture engine is ready by every live EIS: ready 2036, NGSA EIS 2037, S2 fps EIS 2055;
(2) the gear and core stay P&W modules under P&W type data (published term 2). The brief shows no breach.

ANSWERS TO CALIO'S ASKS
1. Proposal: hold, hold. Confirmed.

2. In-service record. The brief and bulletin carry no fleet data: no time on wing, no hot-and-harsh or severe-environment results, no life-limited-part lives, no AOG count and no turn times. The board does not model durability. So I can't tell you the fleet is where it needs to be [PX-0022], and I won't tell you there's no surprise coming. I said that in June 2023, five weeks before the recall [PX-0112][PX-0290].
- The public record shows only that nothing public has happened. No P&W fleet, AOG or quality event appears in any bulletin from 2037 to 2044. P&W's NGSA flow rose from about 8 engines (2037) to about 800 (2044), derived from the public shares (inference). None of that proves durability.
- To the Governance and Public Policy Committee I bring the data as they exist:
(a) time on wing against plan, cooler against hot-and-sandy operators, as I split it in 2023 [PX-0122];
(b) removal intervals against Block D and the Advantage [PX-0116][P-0785];
(c) severe-environment and fleet-leader findings (inference);
(d) every life-limited part's life against full life, with any life-limit reduction [PX-0128];
(e) configuration percentages, AOG count, shop-visit rate, turn times and the pacing parts, run daily and reported weekly [PX-0123][PX-0131].
If the data show a shortfall, the disclosure says so.

3. Readiness. Confirmed. The engine has been ready since 2036 (launch + 6, carried over at the fold).
- NGSA: code 7, EIS 2037, in service.
- S2: a 10-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2055 on code 7, which includes P&W. 2036 is earlier than 2055, a 19-year margin. A 7-year fps (2052) or an Embraer fps (2055) passes too.
- There is no readiness gap anywhere on the board.
- Advice: what we offer Boeing is the standard in service. A newer block would be a new development with its own durability proof, and I promise none.

4. Parts, spares and capacity.
Counted flow (brief section 1):
- 816 (2036), 580 (2037, -29%), 639, 668, 694, 826 (2041, +132, +19%, the largest step), 821, 834, 936 (2044, +102, peak, +15% on 2036), 892 (2045), then 876 from 2046 (-6% off peak, flat).
- That is under the 2035 projection: 2044 at 936 against 976 (-4%), and 876 against 920 from 2047 (-5%).

Mix (derived from public shares, inference):
- GTF OE on the A320neo held at about 440-615 a year in 2037-40 and fell to about 136 by 2044.
- The NGSA engine went from about 8 to about 254 (2040), then to about 800 (2044).
- So the 2037-40 dip was a mix shift, not a lull. The window I named in 2035 was narrower than I said, and that's on me.

Gear and core (inference):
- Under our own terms only P&W makes the gear and core, and every NGSA Joint Venture engine is GTF2's tested configuration until a Rolls-Royce block passes its gate. So our gear and core sit in the Rolls-Royce-credited engines too.
- That module flow rose from about 588 (2037) to about 1,736 (2044), roughly three times, while the counted flow rose 61%. It runs at about 1,750 a year from 2046 (876 each).
- The pacing parts and spares for the gear and core must be sized to that, not to 876.
- The brief has no parts count, so I can't show that capacity covered the climb. I fall short on evidence, and I say so [PX-0066].

Shops:
- The GTF fleet built since 2026 is about 12,100 engines (816 a year for 2026-36, plus about 3,126 for 2037-44, derived). It is ageing into heavy visits.
- The NGSA fleet is about 3,600-3,800 engines by end-2045 and about 8,000 by 2050 (derived).
- I have no time-on-wing data to date the NGSA engine's first shop-visit wave, and I won't guess.

Allocation:
- Fleet spares stay ahead of OE and block hardware when they compete for parts [PX-0080][PX-0123].
- From about 2046 the A320neo GTF OE is gone, so the contest is NGSA OE against two fleets in the shops.
- We agree OE allocation with Airbus jointly [PX-0099] and tell them early where we fall short [PX-0066].
- We fix forward. The Hot Section kit goes into GTF shop visits at value [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100]. Any NGSA durability fix enters as a shop-visit kit under configuration control, after its own test.

5. The Rolls-Royce block gate, held to the Advantage rule.
(a) Configuration control. GTF2's tested configuration stays the type standard. Any Rolls-Royce module change is a new block under a joint configuration board, with P&W sign-off on every interface to the gear and core.
(b) Spares. No intermix in shop visits until the block is certified and its own spares are stocked. GTF2-standard spares are never drawn down for block hardware.
(c) Testing. At least Advantage-level testing (3x the base programme [PX-0084]) at representative severe-environment, hot-and-sandy conditions [PX-0128][PX-0122]. Endurance testing must show time on wing no worse than the fitted standard, with interface load tests on our gear and core.
(d) Full life. Every Rolls-Royce life-limited part has full life at entry into service [PX-0128].
(e) Production and support. Rolls-Royce parts capacity is qualified before rate, because powder metal came from a capacity ramp [P-1040]. Its partner-shop support is in place before entry into service.
(f) The route. The data, not a plan, go to the committee. The block enters service only after the committee clears it. No date is given, and if the data are late, the block waits.

6. Joint Venture governance. Published terms 1 and 2: each partner owns its modules, a joint integration and test team works the interfaces (the team mirrors the architecture [P-1240]), and the gear and core are P&W modules under P&W type data, with no licence, data access or transfer [P-1233]. The brief shows no breach. I can't audit the Joint Venture's internals from it.

Rolls-Royce's two statements, 'the folded UltraFan keeps its own test programme through to entry into service' and its separate UltraFan offer to Boeing, read two ways:
- as Rolls-Royce modules entering as a later block through our gate; or
- as a separate narrowbody engine, named by product and with its own test programme, kept alive under the Joint Venture label.
On the board, UltraFan NB folded and Rolls-Royce's narrowbody engine is the Joint Venture engine. Off the board, I can't tell, and we state no Rolls-Royce intention as fact.
- The technical tell: a block that brings its own gear or core is not a block on our engine. That would be the alignment break [P-1875] and a Board-level risk.
- What settles it: Rolls-Royce confirms in writing that UltraFan content enters only as a block on the Joint Venture engine, through the joint team and our gate, and that any Boeing offer is the Joint Venture engine.

7. Engineering load (advice; no strain charge on this board).
- Fleet support: about 12,100 GTF engines and the growing NGSA fleet.
- Block integration: interface work only. Rolls-Royce's modules are Rolls-Royce's.
- The Boeing offer: the in-service standard, with no work until a launch.
None of it pulls from fleet support if the integration team is staffed separately. A Boeing-specific block would be a new development: one at a time, after the fleet, and to Finance.

8. Veto check: no veto.
- Ground 1: no Rolls-Royce block, no EIS date and no durability claim appears in the orders or in your draft.
- Ground 2: no launch or new commitment is ordered, and the brief shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem.
Watch items are listed under vetoes.

9. Disclosure check: it passes. No durability is claimed beyond the data, no EIS date is given, the Boeing line is a condition, and the GTF2 lines are retired. Three edits:
(a) 'CFM has a new engine in service': the record says 'ready since 2041'. Say 'ready' or 'a new engine'.
(b) 'Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block' should read 'Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block', so that it reads as our term and not as Rolls-Royce's intention.
(c) Keep 'we are sizing parts, spares and shop capacity'. Don't upgrade it to 'sized' until I can show the gear-and-core count.
Counsel reviews the GTF paragraph.

My record is one event, June 2023, and it is silent on Joint Ventures. Items 5 to 7 are seat doctrine and inference.

tests.name: Readiness and durability by EIS (veto ground 1)
tests.threshold: Binding: each engine's ready year is no later than the EIS of the airframe it serves. The Joint Venture engine is ready 6 years after formation, or at the ready year of a folded solo programme if that is earlier (rules.md).
tests.numbers: GTF2: launched 2030, ready 2036 (launch + 6), folded in 2035. Joint Venture formed 2035: formation + 6 would be 2041, but it inherits GTF2's 2036 (bulletin: ready since 2036). UltraFan NB (ready 2037) also folded. NGSA: code 7, EIS 2037, in service; 2036 is no later than 2037. S2: Boeing 10-year fps launched 2045, code 7, EIS 2055; 2036 is no later than 2055. A 7-year fps (2052) or an Embraer fps (2055) also passes. No readiness gap on the board. Grid row 'GTF2: hold': -0.14 (S1) / -0.73 (S2), and readiness holds in both columns.

tests.name: Durability margin before EIS (advice only, not a veto ground)
tests.threshold: About 1 year between ready year and EIS (inference from the Advantage certification slip and the profile's derivative slip prior)
tests.numbers: NGSA: 1 year (2036 to 2037), now history. S2 fps: 19 years (2036 to 2055), with about 18 years of NGSA service behind it by then. Advice: the standard on offer is the in-service standard. Any newer block for an fps is a new development with its own proof, and none is promised.

tests.name: Full life at entry into service and the disclosure rule
tests.threshold: All life-limited parts at full life at EIS; no public EIS promise; no durability claim beyond the data
tests.numbers: Orders are hold and hold. Calio's draft gives no EIS date, claims no durability for the NGSA engine ('we will report that engine's durability as the in-service data show it'), and states full-life parts and proven durability as conditions for any Rolls-Royce block and any new airframe. The 2035 line 'GTF2 ... due to be ready in 2036 ... carrying it through' is retired.

tests.name: In-service durability record of the NGSA engine (time on wing, hot-and-harsh, life-limited parts)
tests.threshold: Claim only what in-service data show; data to the Governance and Public Policy Committee
tests.numbers: Not testable, and not a pass. The brief and bulletin carry no time on wing, severe-environment results, life-limited-part lives, AOG count or turn times, and the board does not model durability. Public record: no P&W fleet, AOG or quality event in any bulletin from 2037 to 2044. P&W's NGSA flow was about 8 (2037), 24, 80, 254, 421, 584, 701, about 800 (2044), derived from public shares (inference). That shows only that nothing public happened, not durability. The committee package: time on wing by environment, removal intervals against Block D and the Advantage, life-limited-part lives, configuration percentages, AOG count and turn times, and the pacing parts.

tests.name: Pacing parts and capacity (veto ground 2)
tests.threshold: If the brief or bulletin shows a live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem, the fleet comes first and an unconditional launch fails. If none is shown, pass, noting that the board does not model parts.
tests.numbers: No launch or new commitment ordered, and no live P&W problem in the 2045 bulletin or brief. Counted NB engines (brief section 1): 816 (2036), 580 (2037), 639, 668, 694, 826 (2041, +132, +19%, the largest step), 821, 834, 936 (2044, peak), 892 (2045), 876 from 2046. Against the 2035 projection: 936 against 976 (-4%) and 876 against 920 (-5%). Derived (inference): A320neo GTF OE was about 572, 615, 588, 440 (2037-40), falling to about 136 (2044). Every Joint Venture engine carries P&W gear and core (term 2, and the GTF2 standard until a Rolls-Royce block is proven). So the gear-and-core flow is about 588 (2037), 948 (2040), 1,247 (2041), 1,736 (2044) and about 1,750 a year from 2046. Shop base: about 12,100 GTF engines delivered since 2026, plus about 3,600-3,800 NGSA engines by end-2045 and about 8,000 by 2050. The brief has no parts count, so capacity against the gear-and-core flow cannot be shown. That is advice, not a veto. Fleet spares stay ahead of OE and block hardware.

tests.name: Contain first
tests.threshold: If a quality escape is in the brief, contain it with a recovery plan before any new commitment
tests.numbers: No quality escape or AOG wave in the 2045 bulletin or brief. No new commitment is ordered.

tests.name: Engineering load (advice only; no strain charge on this board)
tests.threshold: One new development at a time; fleet support is never drawn down for new work
tests.numbers: No new development on the board, and new R&D in 2045 is $0. The load is fleet support (about 12,100 GTF engines since 2026 plus the NGSA fleet), interface work for any Rolls-Royce block (its modules are its own) and the Boeing offer (the in-service standard, with no work until a launch). None pulls from fleet support if the joint integration team is staffed separately. A Boeing-specific block would be a new development: one at a time, after the fleet.

tests.name: Architecture and Joint Venture technical terms
tests.threshold: The engine extends the GTF; P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and core as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence, data access or transfer (company red line)
tests.numbers: Fitted standard: GTF2's tested configuration, a GTF derivative. Published terms 1 and 2 are in force, and the brief shows no breach. Watch items: Rolls-Royce's request for 'terms that credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings', and 'the folded UltraFan keeps its own test programme through to entry into service' alongside its separate UltraFan offer to Boeing. These read as a later block or as a separate narrowbody engine. A block that brings its own gear or core is not a block on our engine: that is the alignment break and a Board-level risk. Get Rolls-Royce's confirmation in writing.

tests.name: Rolls-Royce block durability gate (veto ground 1, watch)
tests.threshold: No Rolls-Royce block enters service before its own durability proof and full-life life-limited parts reach the Governance and Public Policy Committee

Gate: joint configuration board with P&W interface sign-off; no intermix until the block is certified and its spares are stocked; at least 3x base-programme testing at severe-environment conditions; time on wing no worse than the fitted standard; interface load tests on the gear and core; full-life parts at EIS; capacity qualified before rate; support in place before EIS; data to the committee. No date is given, and if the data are late, the block waits.

tests.name: Single aisle

tests.numbers: No widebody move is proposed, and this board has none for P&W.

tests.name: Cancel check (my record is silent)

tests.numbers: Cancel is not legal: GTF2 folded in 2035, and the Joint Venture engine is ready and in service.

tests.name: Disclosure readiness check on Calio's draft
tests.threshold: Every durability word must be supported by the in-service data; the Boeing line must be a condition, not a forecast; no airframer dates; no Rolls-Royce intention stated as fact
tests.numbers: It passes with three edits. (a) 'CFM has a new engine in service': the bulletin says 'ready since 2041'. (b) 'Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block' becomes 'Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block'. (c) Keep 'we are sizing parts, spares and shop capacity', and don't upgrade it to 'sized'. 'Ready since 2036' and 'in service since 2037' are public facts. Ground 1: the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, against NGSA's 2037 EIS and S2's 2055, and no Rolls-Royce block, EIS date or durability claim is ordered or stated. Ground 2: no launch or new commitment is ordered, and the brief shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
1. In-service data showing the NGSA engine short on time on wing, hot-and-sandy shortfalls, or a life-limit reduction on any life-limited part. Then we contain first. Fleet lift goes ahead of NGSA OE and any block hardware, the committee gets the data, the disclosure drops to what the data show, and every Rolls-Royce block waits.
2. A later bulletin showing an AOG wave or a quality escape. Then we contain it and give a recovery plan before any new commitment, with a date only once the parts count supports one, and ground 2 applies to any new launch.
3. Rolls-Royce confirming UltraFan as a separate narrowbody engine, asking for gear or core data or a licence, or pressing to put its content into service before its proof. Ground 1 then binds on any P&W order or statement that supports it, the gear-and-core red line is engaged, and it goes to the Board as an alignment risk.
4. A parts count showing gear-and-core capacity or spares short of the whole Joint Venture flow (about 1,750 a year) or of the GTF shop load. Then spares come first and OE waits for qualified capacity.
5. A Boeing launch that asks for a newer block rather than the in-service standard. That is a new development: one at a time, after the fleet, with its own durability proof and to Finance. Readiness of the in-service standard already passes.
ops.memo:
Bad number first: minus 0.14 booked, minus 0.73 if Boeing launches. No order moves it. Both fields offer only hold. I propose hold, hold.

Second bad number: I have no fleet data. The brief carries no time on wing, no hot-and-sandy results, no life-limited-part lives, no AOG count. So we claim nothing. I won't tell the committee there's no surprise coming. I said that once, five weeks before the recall. I bring the data as they exist: time on wing by environment, removal intervals, life-limited parts, configuration percentages, AOG and turn times, the pacing parts.

Readiness passes. Ready since 2036, NGSA in service since 2037, and a Boeing fps launched now enters service in 2055.

Parts. We delivered 936 engines in 2044, 892 this year and 876 from 2046, under the 976 and 920 we planned for. But under our own terms every Joint Venture engine carries our gear and core, so that module flow was about 1,736 in 2044 and runs about 1,750 a year. Size the pacing parts and spares to that. About 12,100 GTF engines delivered since 2026 are coming into shop visits. Spares come first.

Rolls-Royce block: the Advantage rule. Severe-environment testing, full-life parts, capacity qualified before rate, data to the committee. Late data, the block waits.

Rolls-Royce's 'own test programme' and its separate UltraFan offer read two ways. Get it in writing.

No veto. My record is one event, June 2023, before the recall, and silent on Joint Ventures. This is seat doctrine.

other_moves.move: Fleet first: the Joint Venture engine on NGSA and the GTF fleet; Hot Section kit sold at value; fleet spares ahead of new hardware
other_moves.detail:
The fleet comes before any new hardware [PX-0080][PX-0084].
- The GTF Hot Section durability upgrade stays on offer to operators through our MRO network at value. It is sold, not given away, and it is not tied to any airframe campaign [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100].
- Fleet spares and MRO material are allocated ahead of NGSA OE and ahead of any Joint Venture block hardware when they compete for the same parts.
- We fix forward through shop-visit upgrades. Any durability fix for the NGSA engine enters as a shop-visit kit under configuration control, after its own test.
- Pacing parts and spares for the gear and the core are being sized to every Joint Venture engine that carries them, not only to our counted share, and to the GTF fleet coming into heavy shop visits.
- OE allocation is agreed jointly with Airbus, and we tell Airbus early where we fall short [PX-0099][PX-0066].
No date is given for any ramp or recovery. The move has no effect on the game board.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture governed to its published terms; 'never' restated as the public floor
other_moves.detail:
The formed Joint Venture runs to the terms we published in 2035, restated with one change: the Finance routing comes out of the public text.
(1) The partners share risk and investment equally. Each designs, makes and supports its own modules end to end, and a joint integration and test team works the interfaces.
(2) P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence, no data access and no transfer [P-1233].
(3) A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share. It is never credited with P&W technology, and never with cash beyond equal shares.
(4) The engine in service is GTF2's tested configuration. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block, and it would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life.
Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions. No date is given for any block.

other_moves.move: Standing offer to Boeing's next single-aisle and to Airbus: the in-service Joint Venture engine, on standard terms, no launch-style discounts
other_moves.detail:
This answers Boeing's standing invitation to all three engine makers. We offer the Joint Venture engine, which has been ready since 2036, in the standard now in service. It is offered on standard commercial terms, with no launch discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100], and the same terms apply on NGSA.
- On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven, the contract condition Boeing has set.
- A newer block would be a new development with its own durability proof. None is promised.
- A rival's price, including CFM's new engine and its Embraer partnership, does not move the offer.
- Nothing is said on either airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062], and nothing is aimed at Boeing's timing either way.

other_moves.move: In-service durability report and the Rolls-Royce block gate to the Governance and Public Policy Committee
other_moves.detail:
Eddy brings the data as they exist, and says so plainly where they do not yet exist:
(a) time on wing against plan, split by operating environment;
(b) removal intervals against Block D and the Advantage;
(c) severe-environment and fleet-leader findings;
(d) every life-limited part's life against full life, with any life-limit reduction;
(e) configuration percentages, AOG count, shop-visit rate, turn times and the pacing parts, run daily and reported weekly.
If the data show a shortfall, the disclosure says so, and we contain the problem before any new commitment.

The Rolls-Royce block gate, held to the Advantage rule:
- Configuration control: a joint configuration board, with P&W sign-off on every interface to the gear and core.
- Spares: no intermix in shop visits until the block is certified and its own spares are stocked.
- Testing: at least Advantage-level testing (3x the base programme) at severe-environment conditions [PX-0084][PX-0128]. Time on wing must be no worse than the fitted standard, with interface load tests on our gear and core.
- Parts: full-life parts at entry into service.
- Supply and support: Rolls-Royce's parts capacity qualified before rate, and its support in place before entry into service.
The data go to the committee, and the block waits for its clearance. No date is given. If the data are late, the block waits.

other_moves.move: Annual whole-programme NPV review to the Finance Committee
other_moves.detail:
From Mitchill's memo.

(a) Booked figure: -0.14 = engine value +1.86 less R&D 2.00, charged undiscounted. 'Capitalise on the GTF' is reported as not met.

(b) The bridge from +0.48 (2035) is -0.62, all of it engine value. As PV at 2026:
- 2037-41: +0.11;
- 2042-44: -0.18 (936 engines against 976 in 2044);
- 2045-56: -0.56 (876 a year against 920).
Derived reading of the public tables, labelled inference: the fold and the equal-share rule cost nothing against the S1 path (our 2041 NGSA share of 38.4% matches the projection). From 2042, CFM's ducted engine and its Embraer partnership took about 3.9 pp of NGSA, half of it from us. That is about 44 engines a year.

(c) The end-state share of 23.3% is derived as 876 engines out of 3,768 NB engines (NGSA at 100 a month plus the MAX at 57, all CFM). Against the 2035 S4 projection (+2.63) the gap is -2.77. The +2.15 that S4 projected never showed: 2041 came in at exactly the S1 figure.

(d) S2 sits -0.59 below S1. A Boeing fps puts NGSA under the two-airframe share rule while the MAX stays on CFM, and the fps's P&W slot enters service only in 2055, against an NB count that ends in 2056. The brief has no S2 year table, so the gap cannot be placed by year.

(e) Comparisons:
- Against a buyback (PV 0): -0.14, not met.
- Against Do Nothing: no row in this brief. The direction only: from 2046 all 876 engines a year fly on NGSA.
- Derived return with R&D discounted at 10% (ratable $0.33B a year over 2030-35): about +0.77, with a range of +0.49 to +1.01. Labelled derived, for Finance only, never booked and never public.

other_moves.move: Enterprise risk register update to the Audit Committee and the full Board

Retire the 2035 risk that Airbus moves NGSA to code 5. It is moot: NGSA is in service with P&W fitted.

(1) In-service durability and time on wing of the NGSA engine. It now holds the credibility objective, and no fleet data are yet in the brief.
(2) Share pressure from CFM's ducted engine and its Embraer partnership.
(3) Joint Venture alignment with Rolls-Royce: its 'own test programme' for the folded UltraFan and its separate UltraFan offer to Boeing.

other_moves.move: Written alignment confirmation sought from Rolls-Royce; any cash or block cost to Finance as a capital item

We ask Rolls-Royce to confirm in writing two things. First, that UltraFan content enters only as a later block on the Joint Venture engine, through the joint team and our gate. Second, that any Boeing offer it makes is the Joint Venture engine.

A block that brings its own gear or core is not a block on our engine. It would be the alignment break, and a Board-level risk [P-1875].

Any Rolls-Royce request for a technology credit in cash beyond equal shares, any block integration cost beyond equal shares, and any fleet-cost overrun return to Finance as a capital item. Mitchill would veto the first on ground 3. This routing stays in the private record.

decision.public_statement:
Bad news first. The new single-aisle market is more contested than when we committed. CFM's new engine has been ready since 2041, and CFM has a partnership with Embraer. We have no birthright on any aircraft, and we earn our place every day. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. The fleet work goes on. The Hot Section durability upgrade is offered to GTF operators through our MRO network, and fleet spares come ahead of new hardware.

We control what we can control. The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, built on GTF2's tested configuration, has been ready since 2036. It is fitted on Airbus's new single-aisle, which has been in service since 2037. Time on wing is the name of the game. We will report that engine's durability as the in-service data show it, and not ahead of them. We are sizing parts, spares and shop capacity to the fleet we support, the GTF and the new engine together.

The Joint Venture shares risk and investment equally. It never shares our core technology. Pratt & Whitney designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules, under its own type data. A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share, never through ours. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block. It would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions.

Our engine is on offer to any new single-aisle, Boeing's included, on standard terms, with no launch discounts. On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates.

The dividend comes first. This year's plan needs no new engine development spending and no change to the dividend or to our path on debt.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo hold; jv_with_rr hold. Both are the only legal values (brief section 3), and both are the default, so nothing goes to the Board. premium_b is 0 and overrides is empty.

THE TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP:

(1) Start from Eddy's proposal. He proposes hold and hold, and Mitchill recommends the same.

(2) Strike any plan that fails a binding veto. None does.
- Mitchill: ground 1 (dividend and debt) is not engaged at $0 of new R&D. Ground 2 (unselected engine) is not applicable, because no live GTF2 exists and the Joint Venture engine is selected and fitted on NGSA. Ground 3 (terms) passes. Ground 4 (upside) passes.
- Mitchill's two conditional vetoes, on a partner credit beyond equal shares and on overclaiming in the disclosure, are not engaged. I took his wording fixes into the statement: 'no new engine development spending'; 'CFM's new engine has been ready since 2041'; 'any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block'.
- Eddy: both grounds pass. The engine has been ready since 2036, against NGSA's 2037 and S2's 2055, and no block, date or durability claim appears. His watch item is not triggered. I took his edits: 'Under the Joint Venture's terms'; 'sizing', not 'sized'.

(3) Safety and durability set the constraint [PX-0035][PX-0073]. No Rolls-Royce block enters service before its own proof and full-life parts reach the Governance and Public Policy Committee, and GTF2's tested configuration stays the fitted standard until then. Eddy has no fleet data to show, so the disclosure claims no durability for the NGSA engine. It says we will report it as the data show it.

(4) Optimise. There is one row: 'GTF2: hold', -0.14 (S1) / -0.73 (S2). It is the best grid plan in both columns because it is the only one.

(5) Tie-breaks. 'The fleet beats a new engine' governs the other moves. 'Miss a cycle' does not apply: the Joint Venture engine is already ready for any code that includes us, and S2 is code 7. A rival's discount moves nothing.

WEIGHTS: S1 0.60, S2 0.40. I move from my framing 0.65/0.35 to Mitchill's and the Board's 0.40.
- For S2: Boeing's NB delivery share fell from 40.1% to 26.6%, its balance sheet is repaired, and its sourcing move names code 7. Those are lead indicators.
- My own incrementalism on a rival's timing [PX-0093] pulls me low, and Mitchill books downside early.
- Expected PV: 0.6 x -0.14 + 0.4 x -0.73 = -0.376, reported as -0.38. Worst column: S2, -0.73.
- The row is negative at any weights, and nothing on the orders turns on them.
- I say nothing on Boeing's dates [PX-0062], and nothing we do is aimed at its timing either way.

THE HONEST ACCOUNT (Mitchill's numbers; I trust his cash over my dates):
- The booked -0.14 is engine value +1.86 less R&D 2.00, charged undiscounted.
- The -0.62 since 2035 is all engine value, a step, not timing. Through 2041 we ran at or above plan. From 2042, CFM's ducted engine and its Embraer partnership took about 3.9 pp of NGSA, half from us. That is about 44 engines a year: 920 became 876. The attribution is derived inference from public tables.
- Our 2035 grid had no CFM column. The +2.15 that S4 projected never showed.
- S2 is -0.59 below S1 because the two-airframe share rule cuts Airbus's preference while the MAX stays on CFM, and the fps's P&W slot enters service only in 2055, against an NB count that ends in 2056. The fps volume beyond 2056 is real in 'miss a cycle' terms [PX-0071], but it is RTX-wide in my record, inferred here, and not booked.
- The derived WACC-discounted figure (about +0.77) goes to Finance only. It is never booked and never public.

DISCLOSURE: the GTF2 'due ready 2036 ... carrying it through' lines are retired as history. 'Responsible bets with responsible paybacks' [PX-0010] is dropped, because -0.14 does not support it. The Boeing line is a condition, not a forecast. 'Never' is the public floor on technology credit, and the Finance routing moves to the private record. Counsel reviews the GTF paragraph.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD: my record is Low on the Rolls-Royce Joint Venture. Its governance, the block gate and the alignment request follow company doctrine [P-1233][P-1240][P-1875], Eddy's seat doctrine and Mitchill's cash test. I defer to Eddy on readiness, parts and capacity.

BIASES WATCHED:
- Operating-date optimism: no block, ramp or recovery date is given.
- Architecture loyalty: GTF2's configuration stays the standard only until Rolls-Royce's proof is in, not as pride.
- Incrementalism on Boeing: I corrected toward Mitchill's 0.40.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighed heavily, as the team rule and my profile direct: I trust Mitchill's cash numbers over my own operating dates.
- Adopted: his weights (0.60/0.40), the expected PV of -0.38 and S2 as the worst column, the envelope check ($0 new R&D, GTF2's $2.0B covering our $2B share, no fold write-off), and the dividend and debt confirmation.
- His NPV bridge goes to the Finance Committee as written. The -0.62 is a step from CFM's moves from 2042, not timing. The S4 +2.15 never showed. The end-state 23.3% is derived.
- His candour that the 2035 grid had no CFM column, and that the low end was put in the wrong place, is the account I own.
- His explanation of S2 corrects mine on two points: Airbus's free slots, and the possibility that part of the gap sits in delivered years.
- His wording fixes are all taken, and his advice on term (3) is taken: 'never' stays public, the routing goes private.
- His two conditional vetoes (ground 3 on any partner credit beyond equal shares, ground 4 on any overclaim) are respected and not engaged.
- The derived +0.77 stays labelled, for Finance only.

frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin, round 3, decision year 2045)
- NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, in service since 2037. Code 7: RR, P&W and CFM all fitted. Airbus certifies each engine as it matures, and its A320neo lines run longer on the Alt plan.
- The Joint Venture formed in 2035, once P&W and Rolls-Royce had both committed. Its engine has been ready since 2036; it took the schedule of a folded solo programme. Our UltraFan NB Solo (2030) and P&W's GTF2 Solo (2030) both folded into it in 2035.
- P&W's public terms:
  - equal shares;
  - each partner designs, makes and supports its own modules;
  - GTF2's tested configuration enters service first;
  - Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block, after its own durability proof;
  - no Joint Venture engine enters service until durability is proven and life-limited parts have full life.
  Those are P&W's words. We speak only for our own decisions.
- CFM/GE:
  - GEnx upgrade ready since 2033. It is why RR widebody share fell 2.8 pp in 2042.
  - CFM ducted engine (2035) ready since 2041; the CFM-Embraer partnership ready since 2042.
  - RISE remains a technology programme, with no product and no date. Under the rules an Open Fan can be ready no earlier than 2045, so a launch this round would be ready in 2055.
- Boeing:
  - no fps and no date ('the case isn't there yet');
  - no 787 Re-engine ('the most efficient airplane in its class'; Charleston capacity added);
  - its sourcing plan names code 7 (CFM, GTF2 and UltraFan NB) and makes durability proven before entry into service a contract condition;
  - 737 held at 57 a month.
- Airbus: widebody focus on the A350 family and the A350F. No A350 Re-engine.
- No 787 or A350 Re-engine of any kind is on the record.
- Observed 2044:
  - narrowbody deliveries: Boeing 458, Airbus 1,266 (26.6% / 73.4%);
  - narrowbody engines: CFM 49.6%, P&W 27.1%, RR 23.2%;
  - widebody engines: CFM/GE 44.8%, RR 55.2%.

OUR POSITION (brief section 1)
- ΔPV +9.61, yield 108.74% (enterprise value $110B, WACC 10%). Engine value +15.32, R&D -4.00 (our Joint Venture share), write-off -1.71 (the Solo's spend beyond our share, folded in 2035).
- Narrowbody engine share: 0.3% in 2037, 9.7% in 2040, 19.4% in 2042, 25.1% in 2045, 23.3% from 2047. That is 872 engines in 2045 and 876 a year from 2046.
- Widebody engine share: 58.0% to 2041, then 55.2% from 2042 (188 engines a year).
- Narrowbody development spend has ended. No programme cash is outstanding.

OBJECTIVE STATUS (brief section 2)
- Enter the narrowbody market: MET (25.1% in 2045, 23.3% in 2050).
- Keep widebody dominance: MET (55.2% at the low point, 5.2 pp above the line).
- Bounded narrowbody risk (at most $4B): NOT MET. It is locked at $5.71B, and no order this round changes it.
- Widebody never starved: MET at $0 strain. It holds only while both widebody items stay at hold.

GRID COLUMNS
- S1: rivals hold.
- S2: Boeing launches the fps (10-year variant) on code 5.
- S3: 787 Re-engine.
- S4: 787 and A350 Re-engines.
- Hold row: +9.61 / +9.62 / +9.61 / +9.86. It is the best row in every column. S2 adds only +0.01, because a 2055 entry into service barely counts by 2056.

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto follows our decision). Risk appetite 4 of 5.
- It expects Do Nothing on all four fields.
- It would veto:
  - `t1000_upgrade: launch` (-6.48, more than double the $3B cap);
  - `ultrafan_wb: launch` (no Re-engine on the record; -8.02 to -9.00, against a $1B sub-cap);
  - any launch without McCabe's co-signature, with a binding Civil veto standing, or with an override.
- It wants the round-2 review items closed, the statement updated and the objectives stated plainly.
