vetoes.plan: Any concession or launch discount to win the Boeing fps or widebody share (an other move; none is proposed)
vetoes.ground: This is a standing condition on my support, not a veto of the CEO's proposal. S2 is worth $0.01B (about £7m) to the hold row, so there is nothing to concede. If a concession appears in the other moves, I withhold my support.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Delivered numbers and an announced customer would change my view.
- A Re-engine on the record: if a 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the bulletin, I re-test one widebody row, A350 first, on that round's grid. The upgrade would need at least +$3B before the strain in every plausible column. UltraFan WB would need +$4B weighted before the strain to sit within its $1B sub-cap, and must not lose more than its $4B bill in any plausible column.
- A corrected grid: if the CEO's final orders or a corrected grid show any widebody row above hold in any column, I re-run the hurdle on it.
- Trent durability: if Watson reports a Trent 1000 or Trent 7000 time-on-wing problem, I fund it inside the flat envelope. It becomes a programme only if a priced row clears the bar.
- A Boeing fps launch on code 7 brings a second airframe on the same engine at no new spend. It changes no order.
- A Civil veto from Watson against the final orders or the statement is his ground. I would say so, and the orders stay at hold.
- Weights: none of my votes turns on them.
cfo.memo:
We've always said safety, then the balance sheet. This round is about protecting the cash we have built.

Do Nothing on all four fields is the best row in every column: +9.61 / +9.62 / +9.61 / +9.86. That is +9.62 on weights B, which I confirm, and on my own read; +9.68 uniform. It commits no new programme money. Narrowbody development spend ended at $5.71B: our $4B Joint Venture share and $1.71B written off, all booked in 2035. In 2035 we said formation would save about £1.7bn against the Solo. It did.

I withhold my co-signature on both widebody launches, and that binds. The Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.48 on any weights, worst -6.48 against a $2B bill, and still -1.48 before the strain. UltraFan WB is -8.88 on B, worst -9.00 against a $4B bill, and no Re-engine is on the record. Either one adds the $5B strain for good: about £3.7bn, roughly a year of today's free cash flow guidance. No weighting changes either vote.

S2 is worth $0.01B to us, about £7m, so there is nothing to concede for it.

No balance-sheet trigger is in play.

For 2050, the upgrade would need at least +$3B before the strain in every plausible column. UltraFan WB would need a Re-engine on the record and +$4B weighted. Neither is in sight.

My record is silent on engine-launch economics, so these bars are team doctrine. That's how you should hold it.

tests.name: Ready by EIS (Joint Venture engine on NGSA)
tests.threshold: The Joint Venture engine is ready at formation + 6, or at the earlier date the bulletin shows for a folded programme, no later than the EIS of the airframe that selects it. Zero margin passes with a note. A fail is advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers:
Formed 2035. Ready 2036 on the bulletin. It took the schedule of the folded GTF2 Solo: 2030 + 6 = 2036, P&W's full six years, not compressed. Formation + 6 alone would be 2041, and our folded UltraFan NB would have been 2037 (2030 + 7). NGSA launched 2030 on code 7, EIS 2037: one year of margin. In service since 2037.

In-service record, brief §1:
- RR narrowbody share: 0.3% (2037), 1.0% (2038), 3.2% (2039), 9.7% (2040), 14.3% (2041), 19.4% (2042), 22.2% (2043), 23.2% (2044), 25.1% (2045), 24.1% (2046), 23.3% from 2047.
- Engines: 7, 23, 80, 254, 423, 583, 700, 802, 872 (2045), then 876 a year.
- Cumulative: 3,744 by 2045 and 8,124 by 2050.

Fleet: the bulletin and the brief report no durability, time-on-wing or quality event on the Joint Venture engine. At its 2035 gate Airbus found 'no supply crunch, engine slip or quality event'. The board does not report time on wing, so I have no first-hand fleet data and claim none.

Watch item (public bulletin): P&W's own account of GTF shortfalls (a powder-metal process issue, shop capacity, shorter time on wing in hot and sandy conditions). Under P&W's terms it supports its own modules. Our proof for the Rolls-Royce modules must cover hot and harsh conditions (inference).

tests.name: Ready by EIS (any fps launched this round)
tests.threshold: The engine must be ready by the fps EIS: launch + 7 (launch_7yr) or launch + 10 (launch_10yr, launch_via_embraer).
tests.numbers:
Joint Venture engine ready 2036. A 2045 fps on launch_7yr has EIS 2052 (+16). On launch_10yr or via Embraer it has EIS 2055 (+19). S2 (10-year, code 5): RR is fitted through the Joint Venture engine, and the hold row gains only +0.01 (+9.62 against +9.61), because a 2055 EIS barely counts by 2056.

These fps dates are internal planning dates only and never go public. The Boeing answer must not imply any date for the Rolls-Royce-module block, nor that our modules will be on the fps by its EIS. It must not offer a Solo UltraFan NB: that programme folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 (inference).

tests.name: Ready by EIS (UltraFan WB, if launched: tested to reject)
tests.threshold: UltraFan WB is ready at launch + 6 and counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. It must be ready by that Re-engine's EIS (launch + 5). A fail is advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers: Launched 2045, ready 2051. S1 and S2: no Re-engine, so no airframe to meet. S3 and S4: a 787 Re-engine (and an A350 Re-engine) launched 2045 enters service in 2050, so UltraFan WB misses it by one year. That is why the brief keeps widebody share at 55.2% in 2050 in every column. At most 2051-2061 counts. Because 6 > 5, UltraFan WB meets a Re-engine only if it is launched at least a year before that Re-engine, which in practice means a round earlier (arithmetic, inference). The fail is advice, not a veto. Recommended order: hold.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No statement, public other move or rationale may disclose or count on an EIS or ready date earlier than launch + development years. That means formation + 6 for the Joint Venture (or the bulletin's 2036 for the folded programme), launch + 6 for UltraFan WB, and no date at all for the Rolls-Royce-module block, which its own durability proof gates.
tests.numbers:
CEO's draft statement: 'Rolls-Royce content enters service when its own durability is proven, and not before. We give no date for it.' It says nothing on NGSA's rates, fps dates or Re-engine dates, and it retires the round-2 'no earlier than 2037' without putting a new date in its place. The draft public other moves (Trent time on wing, the partner-shop plan, the Boeing answer, standard terms) carry no dates.

The only engine dates on the public record are the bulletin's: the Joint Venture engine ready 2036, NGSA EIS 2037. The draft repeats neither, and neither is early.

Rationale caution: credit the 23.3% to the Joint Venture engine under the board's equal-share rule, not to Rolls-Royce modules being in service by any year. I re-check the final text at step 4.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale, so a partner-shop support plan must be live before any narrowbody EIS: for the NGSA fleet, before any Rolls-Royce-module block enters service, and before any fps EIS (inference).

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody programme (the Joint Venture) beside a widebody programme (Trent 1000 upgrade or UltraFan WB) costs a one-off $5B of strain. Red lines: no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development; no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected (seat and company rule, inference).
tests.numbers:
Do Nothing: $0 strain in all four columns (brief objective table).

Trent 1000 upgrade: $5B in every column. Item value -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46; before the strain -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.46.

UltraFan WB: $5B in every column. Item value -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02; before the strain -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.28 / -3.02.

The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and cannot be cancelled, so the strain comes from both programmes being on the record ('for good'), not from overlap years. Only cancelling the widebody item before it is ready would remove it: before 2048 for the upgrade, before 2051 for UltraFan WB.

Red lines on the board record: the upgrade-while-in-development rule does not bite, because no UltraFan is in development (the Solo folded in 2035 and the Joint Venture engine is ready). The NB Solo rule is not applicable. Operationally, the Rolls-Royce-module block's durability proof draws on the same engineers, and that is the load the strain prices (inference).

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR engines a year from the brief. The board sets no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable; a narrowbody ramp needs partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity (advice).
tests.numbers:
Narrowbody: 872 engines in 2045 and 876 a year from 2046. Widebody: 188 a year from 2042. Total about 1,064 a year from 2046, against 197 today and my midterm widebody OE ramp of 300-350.

The narrowbody load is 84% of the about 1,040 a year we sized for in round 2, so it holds with margin. The brief reports no constraint.

Under P&W's terms P&W makes the gear and the core, so the gearbox-sizing constraint now sits on its module (inference). Castings and forgings for our modules go to high-performing suppliers (GBP 685M of GBP 2.5B in 2023).

For widebody shop-visit load I use my figure, 1,100-1,200 a year, not McCabe's 1,400-1,500 definition. The narrowbody shop-visit wave goes through partner shops.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
Every held row, every column: 58.0% (2040), 55.2% (2045), 55.2% (2050). The low point is 55.2%, 5.2 pp above the line, and the 2.8 pp step in 2042 is the GEnx upgrade.

The upgrade would count from 2048 (2045 + 3) and give 60.0% in 2050. That is not needed, and it is -1.48 before the strain. UltraFan WB leaves 55.2% in every column.

There is no Trent 1000 or Trent 7000 durability reason for a programme: the board reports no time-on-wing event. The answer to GEnx is time on wing inside the flat envelope: longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and 7000, life-limited part extensions, and the at-least-40% time-on-wing aim.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: UltraFan technology feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively; grid values never adjusted.
tests.numbers: UltraFan and the Rolls-Royce-module durability work keep feeding Trent time on wing. This is not priced, and the grid is not adjusted. Holding both widebody items does not stop the Trent fleet work inside the envelope.

vetoes.plan: CEO's proposal: Do Nothing on all four fields (ultrafan_nb_solo hold, jv_with_pw hold, ultrafan_wb hold, t1000_upgrade hold), with the draft statement and the draft other moves
vetoes.ground:
Not invoked. I checked all three Civil grounds.
(a) Maturity: not compressed. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 at P&W's full six years and has been in service on NGSA since 2037. The Rolls-Royce modules keep their own test programme through to EIS.
(b) Early date: the draft gives no date for the Rolls-Royce block and none on NGSA, the fps or any Re-engine.
(c) Support: the partner-shop plan is live and ours before any Rolls-Royce block enters service, and it is sized for a second airframe.
No test fails on the proposed orders.

vetoes.plan: Final statement, public other moves and rationale (re-checked at step 4)
vetoes.ground:
Conditional. I invoke the Civil veto if any of these appears:
(a) Any date, year or 'no earlier than' for the Rolls-Royce-module block or Rolls-Royce content on any airframe, or any date in the Boeing answer.
(b) Anything that counts on our modules entering service by a given year, or on Rolls-Royce content being on the fps at its EIS. The same applies to a design change counted on before its own durability proof.
(c) Any text in which P&W's shops replace our partner-shop plan before a Rolls-Royce block enters service, or a Boeing answer without support in place before EIS.
If invoked, the team rule makes the veto binding: the CEO revises once, within it. The ground rests on attributed transcript turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283).

vetoes.plan: t1000_upgrade: launch
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. On the board it breaks no red line: no UltraFan is in development, since the Solo folded in 2035 and the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036. It adds $5B of strain for good. Item value -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46 against a $2B bill; -1.48 before the strain. Operationally it competes with the Rolls-Royce-module block's durability proof for the same engineers. Advice to hold; the money ground belongs to McCabe and the Board.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_wb: launch
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. Ready by EIS fails (advice): ready 2051 (2045 + 6), against 2050 for any Re-engine launched this round, and no Re-engine is on the record. It adds $5B of strain for good. Item value -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02; -3.02 to -4.00 before the strain. The CEO's red line (no UltraFan WB without a Re-engine on the record) and the Board's would-veto apply. Advice to hold.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Any of these would change my view:
(1) A Rolls-Royce-module gate fails, or a fleet durability or time-on-wing event hits the Joint Venture engine on NGSA. Our block then waits, we tell Airbus and P&W early, and testing never bends to a ramp [R-0970].
(2) The final statement, other moves or rationale carries a date for our block, counts on our modules in service by a year (including on the fps), or lets P&W's shops stand in for our partner-shop plan before our block enters service. That is a binding Civil veto.
(3) A 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the bulletin. I re-test one row, A350 first. UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056 and counts only once a Re-engine is in service; the upgrade launched in 2050 counts from 2053. Each still carries the $5B strain for good.
(4) Trent 1000 or 7000 durability that the in-envelope work (HP turbine blades, life-limited part extensions) cannot hold, or widebody share heading toward 50% on a further GEnx move. That gives the upgrade a durability case to bring as a row, still against its $2B bill plus the strain.
(5) Supplier or partner-shop capacity that falls short of about 876 narrowbody and 188 widebody engines a year, or of the narrowbody shop-visit wave from a fleet of 8,124 by 2050.
(6) Named airline commitments for the Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce content [RX-0297].
ops.memo:
Tufan, Helen: Civil tests, 2045. Do Nothing on all four fields. I concur.

Readiness. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, P&W's full six years from GTF2's 2030 launch, not compressed. NGSA entered service in 2037: one year of margin. Our narrowbody engines: 7 in 2037, 872 this year, 876 a year from 2046. The bulletin shows no fleet durability event. P&W's GTF lesson, time on wing in hot and sandy conditions, is our watch item.

Our block. Rolls-Royce modules keep their own test programme through to entry into service: module rig durability, full-engine endurance including hot and harsh, life-limited parts at full life, certification, then support live. No date. No pacing bent to any ramp. No concession. I report the gates to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee every round.

Support. The partner-shop plan stays live and ours, sized for a second airframe before any fps entry into service. P&W's shops add capacity after, never instead.

Strain. Zero on Do Nothing in every column. Either widebody item adds $5B for good: the upgrade is -6.48, UltraFan WB -8.02 to -9.00, and both lose before the strain. UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2051, a year after any Re-engine launched now.

Widebody. 55.2%, 5.2 points above the line. The lever is time on wing, inside the envelope.

Statement: no date anywhere. Our Boeing offer is our Joint Venture share, not a Solo UltraFan, with support before entry into service.

We're pacing that program properly.

other_moves.move: Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 time-on-wing and durability work continues inside a flat R&D envelope
other_moves.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, and life-limited part extensions on the installed fleet. The money is redeployed inside a broadly flat envelope, not added. This is our answer on the widebody, not a new programme. No widebody programme is launched [RX-0123, RX-0214, RX-0101].

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan through partner shops: live for the NGSA fleet and sized for a second airframe
other_moves.detail: Partner-shop network on the Singapore Joint Venture model, repair technology qualified in those shops, a spare-engine pool and an early-years intervention team. The plan is Rolls-Royce's own. It is in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service, and it is sized for a second airframe before that airframe enters service. Our partner's shops add capacity after that and never replace this plan. No dates are disclosed [RX-0283, RX-0287].

other_moves.move: Answer to Boeing's engine-sourcing invitation, renewed
other_moves.detail: Rolls-Royce offers its part of the Joint Venture engine for a future Boeing single-aisle, on standard terms, with no launch discount and no concession. Durability proven before entry into service, as a contract condition. Support and MRO through partner shops in place before entry into service. No dates and no new spend. Rolls-Royce speaks only for its own part [RX-0058, RX-0081, RX-0283].

other_moves.move: Standard commercial terms only
other_moves.detail: No concessions to buy narrowbody or widebody share. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097].

other_moves.move: Capital allocation frame
other_moves.detail: Cash from the Trent and Joint Venture fleets goes first to the balance sheet, then to a 30-40% dividend payout, then to investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing, through the Investment Committee at mid-to-high-teens hurdles. No equity raise, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions [RX-0242, RX-0213, RX-0215, RX-0261].

other_moves.move: Rolls-Royce-module durability gates reported to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee every round
other_moves.detail: Watson reports the gates with no date: module rig durability, full-engine endurance including hot and harsh conditions, life-limited parts at full life, certification, then support live. Our modules keep their own test programme through to entry into service; no pacing bent to any airframer's ramp; no concession to P&W or any airframer. P&W's GTF hot-and-sandy time-on-wing record is the watch item. If a gate fails, the block waits and we tell Airbus and P&W early [RX-0296, RX-0284, R-1476, R-0970].

other_moves.move: Widebody watch for 2050
other_moves.detail: If a 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the bulletin, the ExCo brings one row, A350 first, on the 2050 grid with its item value, worst column against its own bill and the $5B strain shown. Bars (team doctrine, inference): the upgrade needs at least +$3B before the strain in every plausible column; UltraFan WB needs a Re-engine on the record and at least +$4B weighted before the strain, so its shortfall sits inside the $1B sub-cap, and must not lose more than its $4B bill in any plausible column. Otherwise the core is protected through time on wing.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on Airbus's new single-aisle. Rolls-Royce content enters service when its own durability is proven, and not before. We give no date for it. Our support through partner shops is ours, and it is in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service. Testing does not bend to anyone's date. Our answer to Boeing stands: Rolls-Royce's part of the engine, on standard terms, with durability proven and support in place before entry into service. On the widebody, we look after the Trent fleet through time on wing. No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. There's no change of strategy. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on all four fields. ultrafan_nb_solo hold, jv_with_pw hold, ultrafan_wb hold, t1000_upgrade hold. None of these is a Board item. It is my proposal, both memos recommend it, and nothing struck it.

THE QUESTION, IN CASH AND QUALITY OF EARNINGS [RX-0054]. We made the narrowbody bet, paid for it, and it is earning. The Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA. Our narrowbody share is 25.1% in 2045 and 23.3% from 2047: 872 engines this year, 876 a year after that. Narrowbody development money ended at $5.71B, all booked in 2035: our $4B share plus a $1.71B write-off. Today's ΔPV is +9.61 (engine value +15.32, R&D -4.00, write-off -1.71). Following Watson's caution, I credit the 23.3% to the Joint Venture engine under the equal-share rule, not to Rolls-Royce modules being in service by any year. This round is about protecting those earnings and the widebody franchise, not adding activity.

GRID, COLUMN BY COLUMN. Item value is the row minus 'UltraFan NB: hold'.
- Hold row 'UltraFan NB: hold': +9.61 / +9.62 / +9.61 / +9.86 (S1-S4). Best in every column. Worst column +9.61.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade': row +3.13 / +3.14 / +3.13 / +3.40. Item -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46. With the $5B strain added back, -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.46. Worst column -6.48 against its own $2B bill. Widebody would go from 55.2% to 60.0% in 2050, but 55.2% already clears the line. McCabe puts the extra engines at about +$0.52B of PV against a $2B bill.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB': row +0.61 / +0.62 / +1.33 / +1.84. Item -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02. With the strain added back, -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.28 / -3.02. Worst column -9.00 against its own $4B bill. Widebody stays at 55.2% in every column, because it would be ready in 2051, a year after any Re-engine launched now.
- The two widebody items are exclusive, so there is no joint row. Both narrowbody fields are hold only.

WEIGHTS. There is no selection to weigh. The columns are rivals' moves, so P is 0.1 for 'nothing on the record' (inference). Sets (calculation in /tmp/wargame-rolls_royce/dash-2050-sd/work/r3_decide_calc.py):
- B, the Board's illustrative set, confirmed by McCabe: 0.70 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.05. Hold +9.624; upgrade item -6.479 (-1.479 before strain); UltraFan WB item -8.879 (-3.879).
- C/M, my read and McCabe's: 0.80 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.05. Same votes; hold +9.623.
- U, uniform: hold +9.675; upgrade -6.475; UltraFan WB -8.575.
- R, Re-engine-heavy: 0.40 / 0.10 / 0.25 / 0.25. Hold +9.674; upgrade -6.475; UltraFan WB -8.575.
No set changes any vote. Both widebody items lose in every column, even before the strain.

TESTS.
- Airframers first [RX-0058]: no 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Boeing declined a 787 Re-engine. That fails UltraFan WB outright.
- Four-part gate [RX-0030]: the upgrade fails on the business model (it loses before the strain, and the strain is anti-synergy). UltraFan WB fails on the market and the business model.
- Profitable or not at all [RX-0058]: neither item clears zero.
- Premium cap: the upgrade shortfall (about $6.5B) is more than double the $3B cap. UltraFan WB's ($8.6-8.9B) is far over the $1B sub-cap.
- Reasonable worst case: both items lose more than their own bill in every column.
- Widebody franchise [R-1574]: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 on every held row. The 2.8 pp step in 2042 is the GEnx upgrade. The lever is time on wing, inside the envelope.
- Cash as an input [RX-0042]: Do Nothing commits no new programme money. For the record, capex for either item would be about $0.67B a year (£0.49-0.50bn), plus $5B of strain (about £3.7bn), roughly a year of FY2026 free cash flow guidance.
- My pull toward the 787 ('Why not?' [RX-0117], 'regain market share? Absolutely' [RX-0101]) is real. The grid says why not. The answer is time on wing, not a programme weighed down by a $5B strain.

VETO CHECKS.
- McCabe withholds her co-signature, binding, on t1000_upgrade launch and ultrafan_wb launch. Neither is ordered, so nothing needs revising. Her balance-sheet vetoes are not triggered: no equity, no borrowing, no change in leverage. A fall in the brief's ΔPV is not a trigger.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto on the proposed orders. Maturity is not compressed: the Joint Venture engine took P&W's full six years for GTF2. His conditional veto covers the final statement, the other moves and this rationale. I have written them to his tests: no date, year or 'no earlier than' for the Rolls-Royce block or Rolls-Royce content anywhere; nothing that counts on our modules entering service by a year or being on the fps at its EIS; partner shops are ours, with P&W's shops adding capacity only after, never instead; the Boeing answer is Rolls-Royce's part of the Joint Venture engine, not a Solo UltraFan, with support in place before entry into service; no fps or Re-engine dates go public.

RED-LINE FLAGS.
- McCabe flagged that an ultrafan_wb launch would break the company rule of no UltraFan launch without a programme that can fly it. Struck: not ordered.
- The upgrade breaks no overlap red line on the board, since no UltraFan is in development. It is struck on money grounds alone.
- No cancel is available, and nothing orphaned stands: the Joint Venture flies on NGSA [RX-0051].
- overrides is empty.

OBJECTIVES, PLAINLY.
- Narrowbody entry: met (25.1% in 2045, 23.3% in 2050).
- Widebody dominance: met (55.2% at the low point, 5.2 pp above the line).
- Bounded narrowbody risk (at most $4B): not met, locked at $5.71B (the Solo's 2030-2035 spend, folded into the Joint Venture). No order this round moves it. We accepted that because an airframe selected us.
- Widebody never starved: met at $0 strain, and kept only by holding both widebody items. I will not trade it for a widebody programme that pays on no column.

ROUND-2 BOARD ITEMS: closed or carried; see board_response.

DOCTRINE, NOT RECORD. The column weights, the 2050 widebody bars (upgrade +$3B before the strain in every plausible column; UltraFan WB a Re-engine on the record and +$4B weighted before the strain) and the worst-case rule are team doctrine (inference). On the UltraFan WB bar I take McCabe's +$4B over the Board's +$3B: only +$4B keeps the shortfall inside the Board's own $1B sub-cap.

"We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically." [RX-0058]

memo_weighing.cfo: Weighed heavily, and adopted in full. McCabe confirms weights B as the base and gives her own set M (my set C). Her numbers match mine: hold is +9.624 on B, +9.675 uniform; the upgrade is -6.48 on any weights; UltraFan WB is -8.88 on B and -8.58 on U/R. She withholds her co-signature, binding, on both widebody launches. Neither is ordered, so there is nothing to revise. She confirms no new programme money and that narrowbody spend ended at $5.71B, with the Joint Venture saving about £1.7bn against the Solo, as she said in 2035. She confirms the capital frame and that no balance-sheet trigger is in play. On S2 she shows there is nothing to concede (+$0.01B, about £7m). I take her 2050 bar for UltraFan WB (+$4B weighted before the strain) over the Board's +$3B, because only hers keeps the shortfall inside the $1B sub-cap. Her flag that an UltraFan WB launch would break the no-programme-to-fly-it rule is noted and struck, since it is not ordered.
memo_weighing.ops: Weighed heavily on readiness, support and statement discipline, and adopted in full. Watson concurs with Do Nothing and invokes no Civil veto on the orders. The Joint Venture engine took P&W's full six years for GTF2, not compressed, and is in service on NGSA with no fleet event on the record. P&W's GTF time on wing in hot and sandy conditions is our watch item, and our module proof covers hot and harsh conditions. I wrote the statement, the other moves and the rationale to his conditional veto: no date, year or 'no earlier than' for the Rolls-Royce block; nothing that counts on our modules being in service by a year or on the fps at its EIS; partner shops ours, P&W's adding capacity after, never instead; the Boeing answer is our part of the Joint Venture engine, not a Solo UltraFan. I kept the fps planning gates internal. His capacity read (narrowbody load at 84% of what we sized for in round 2) is advice and holds. His view that the upgrade would compete for the same engineers as our module proof supports the hold.

decision.expected_scenario: S1, rivals hold (about 0.70-0.80). If Boeing launches the fps this round, the 10-year variant on code 7 is likelier than S2's code 5; either way it is worth about +$0.01B to us. A 787 Re-engine is about 0.10, and one with an A350 Re-engine as well about 0.05.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: 'UltraFan NB: hold' (Do Nothing on all four fields): +9.61 in S1. It is the best row in every column (+9.61 / +9.62 / +9.61 / +9.86). The upgrade row (+3.13 in S1) and the UltraFan WB row (+0.61 in S1) are dominated in every column.
decision.premium_reason: The orders are the PV-best row in every column, so there is no premium. For the record, choosing either widebody item would have cost about $6.48B (upgrade, over the $3B cap) or $8.58-8.88B (UltraFan WB, against the $1B sub-cap), and both are rejected.
decision.objective_note: Narrowbody entry is met (25.1% in 2045, 23.3% in 2050). Widebody dominance is met (55.2% at the low point, 5.2 pp above the 50% line). Bounded narrowbody risk is not met: it is locked at $5.71B by the Solo's 2030-2035 spend, folded into the Joint Venture, and no order this round can move it; we accepted that because an airframe selected us. Widebody never starved is met at $0 strain, and it stays met only while both widebody items are held. The GM's scored objective (RR narrowbody share above 0 in 2045 and 2050; RR widebody share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050) is met on the hold row in every column.
decision.predictions:
2045 round, private:
- Boeing launches the fps: about 0.40. If it does, the 10-year variant is likelier (it promised headroom), and code 7 is likelier than code 5, as its sourcing plan says. S2 exactly (10-year, code 5): about 0.05-0.15. Either way about +$0.01B to us, because a late entry into service barely counts by 2056.
- 787 Re-engine: about 0.10 (Boeing called the 787 'the most efficient airplane in its class' and is adding Charleston capacity).
- A350 Re-engine as well: about 0.05 (Airbus's widebody focus is the A350 family and the A350F).
- CFM/GE: an Open Fan launch from RISE is unlikely, about 0.10 ('when an aircraft needs it'). If launched, it is ready no earlier than 2055, off our grid. No further GEnx move expected this round.
- P&W: no further Joint Venture move. Fleet durability first; it keeps offering the Joint Venture and GTF2 on standard terms.
- Airbus: NGSA ramps on code 7, with A320neo lines running alongside.
- Rolls-Royce: ΔPV +9.61 in S1 and +9.86 in S4; expected +9.62 on weights B. Widebody 55.2% in 2050, narrowbody 23.3%, strain $0.

board_response.recommendation: Hold both widebody items and say why in plain numbers; 2050 look-ahead; bring the full row, A350 first, if a Re-engine reaches the bulletin.
board_response.response: Taken up. Both are at hold. The upgrade item is -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46, and -1.48 before the strain. The UltraFan WB item is -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02, and -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.28 / -3.02 before the strain. Each loses more than its own bill in every column, on every weight set (B, C/M, U, R). For 2050: the upgrade would count from 2053 and needs at least +$3B before the strain in every plausible column (today about $0.52B of engine value over a longer window). UltraFan WB would be ready in 2056 and needs a Re-engine on the record. I set its weighted bar at +$4B before the strain, McCabe's figure rather than the Board's +$3B, because only +$4B keeps the shortfall inside your own $1B sub-cap. If a Re-engine reaches the bulletin, you get one row, A350 first, with its worst column against its bill and the strain shown.

board_response.recommendation: Look after the widebody core inside the envelope; Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 time-on-wing work as a public other move; report time on wing to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee.
board_response.response: Taken up. It is a public other move: longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, and life-limited part extensions, redeployed inside a flat R&D envelope. Watson reports time on wing to the Committee. The franchise test is not triggered (55.2% at the low point, no Re-engine on the record). Only a Re-engine or a fall below 50% reopens a widebody programme.

board_response.recommendation: Safety in the Joint Venture: report on the two formation conditions; partner-shop support stays ours; Watson brings the block's durability gates to the Committee every round.
board_response.response: Taken up. On the first condition, our modules keep their own test programme through to entry into service. The gates are module rig durability, full-engine endurance including hot and harsh conditions, life-limited parts at full life, certification, then support live. No date is disclosed and no pacing is bent to an airframer's ramp. On the second, there is no concession to P&W or to any airframer: equal shares, standard terms. The partner-shop plan is ours and live before any Rolls-Royce content enters service, and P&W's shops add capacity only after. Watson reports the gates to the Committee every round, an internal other move.

board_response.recommendation: Growth is a second airframe on the same engine at no new spend: renew the Boeing answer on standard terms, nothing conceded.
board_response.response: Taken up. The answer is renewed publicly: Rolls-Royce's part of the Joint Venture engine (not a Solo UltraFan), on standard terms, with no launch discount, durability proven and support in place before entry into service, no dates and no new spend. S2 adds +$0.01B (about £7m), so there is nothing worth conceding. McCabe makes that a standing condition of her support.

board_response.recommendation: Keep the capital frame explicit now that narrowbody spend has ended; McCabe to confirm.
board_response.response: Taken up. McCabe confirmed it in her memo, and it is a public other move. Do Nothing commits no new programme money. Cash goes to the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing, through the Investment Committee at mid-to-high-teens hurdles. No equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. No balance-sheet trigger is in play.

board_response.recommendation: Bring the public statement up to date and keep it disciplined.
board_response.response: Taken up. I dropped 'UltraFan is in development ... no earlier than 2037'. The statement now says the Joint Venture engine is in service, Rolls-Royce content enters when its own durability is proven, and we give no date for it. It says nothing on NGSA's rates, fps dates or Re-engine dates. It keeps durability proven and support in place before entry into service, standard terms, and 'no widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table'. It speaks only for Rolls-Royce, not for P&W's terms. Watson's no-date test was applied to the final text.

board_response.recommendation: State the objectives plainly in rationale.
board_response.response: Taken up in rationale and objective_note. Narrowbody entry met (25.1% in 2045, 23.3% in 2050). Widebody met (55.2% at the low point). Bounded narrowbody risk not met, locked at $5.71B by the Solo's 2030-2035 spend folded into the Joint Venture. Widebody never starved met at $0 strain, kept only by holding both widebody items. We accepted the bounded-risk breach because an airframe selected us. We will not trade the strain objective for a widebody programme that pays on no column.

board_response.recommendation: Round-2 review 1: the standing commitment needs a real decision at the 2045 round, with a withdraw if the commit row is below hold.
board_response.response: Closed. P&W put its commitment on the record in 2035 and the Joint Venture formed that round. The 2045 decision the Board feared, a fold of a ready UltraFan charging our $4B share on top of $8B spent, never arose. We spent $5.71B, not $8B or more. jv_with_pw is now hold only: the Joint Venture is formed, ready and cannot be withdrawn. The share equalisation and write-off are already inside the +9.61 hold row.

board_response.recommendation: Round-2 review 2: hold the formation terms to two conditions (own test programme through to entry into service with no joint design change before it; standard terms, no concession) and report on them.
board_response.response: Reported via Watson; both conditions hold. Under P&W's public terms, Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block after its own durability proof, so no P&W design change goes onto our modules before that proof, and our modules keep their own test programme. No date is given. The terms are equal shares and standard, with no concession to P&W or to any airframer. Our support plan stays ours before any Rolls-Royce content enters service.

board_response.recommendation: Round-2 review 3: S2 is the risk that matters; report Watson's ready year against NGSA 2037 and his gates.
board_response.response: Closed. On the bulletin, the Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 on P&W's full six years for GTF2, not compressed. NGSA entered service in 2037 on code 7 with Rolls-Royce fitted, and its code can no longer change. Support was live before entry into service, and the 2035 gate found no supply crunch, engine slip or quality event. The remaining safety reporting is the Rolls-Royce block's gates, which go to the Committee every round.

board_response.recommendation: Round-2 review 4: the Boeing answer; support sized for a second airframe; gearbox, castings and forgings to high-performing suppliers ahead of the ramp.
board_response.response: Carried forward. The Boeing answer is renewed on standard terms. The support plan is sized for a second airframe before any fps entry into service; those planning gates stay internal. The narrowbody load of about 876 engines a year is 84% of the roughly 1,040 we sized for, so capacity holds with margin. Under P&W's terms the gear and the core are P&W's modules. Castings and forgings for our modules stay with high-performing suppliers.

board_response.recommendation: Round-2 review 5: widebody watch for 2045; one row, A350 first, if a Re-engine reaches the bulletin.
board_response.response: Kept. No 787 or A350 Re-engine of any kind is on the record, so there is no row to bring. Both widebody items were tested and rejected on this grid. The watch carries into 2050 with the bars stated above.

board_response.recommendation: Round-2 review 6: keep the public statement disciplined at 2045 (no Joint Venture date beyond formation plus six or the bulletin's own; nothing on NGSA or fps dates; restate the bounded-risk line).
board_response.response: Done. The statement carries no date at all: none for the Joint Venture engine, the Rolls-Royce block, NGSA, the fps or any Re-engine. The bounded-risk line is restated in rationale at $5.71B, not $8.0B, because the Joint Venture formed in 2035.

veto.ground: No veto. The final orders are hold on all four fields: ultrafan_nb_solo hold, jv_with_pw hold, ultrafan_wb hold, t1000_upgrade hold. ops.note:
Veto check, 2045. I concur. I do not invoke the Civil veto, and no order breaks a red line. This note goes to the Board with the decision.

Orders: ultrafan_nb_solo hold, jv_with_pw hold, ultrafan_wb hold, t1000_upgrade hold. None of these is a Board item.

(a) Maturity: not compressed. Note only. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036. On the bulletin it took the folded GTF2 schedule: 2030 + 6, P&W's full six years. NGSA entered service in 2037, so the engine had one year of margin, and it has been in service since 2037. Nothing in the orders shortens a test programme. The Rolls-Royce-module block keeps its own gates, with no date, through to entry into service: module rig durability, full-engine endurance including hot and harsh conditions, life-limited parts at full life, certification, then support live.

(b) Early date: none. Pass. I checked every date in the final text:
- The public statement gives no date for the Joint Venture engine, the Rolls-Royce block, NGSA, the fps or any Re-engine. It retires the round-2 'no earlier than 2037' and puts no new date in its place.
- The four public other moves carry no dates. The Boeing answer offers Rolls-Royce's part of the Joint Venture engine, not a Solo UltraFan, and gives no date.
- The only dates are in the rationale and in a private other move, and none is early: UltraFan WB 2051 (2045 + 6) and 2056 (2050 + 6), the upgrade from 2053 (2050 + 3), and the bulletin's own 2036 and 2037.
- The rationale credits the 23.3% narrowbody share to the Joint Venture engine under the equal-share rule. It does not count on Rolls-Royce modules being in service by any year, or on the fps at its EIS.

(c) Support before EIS: in place. Pass. The partner-shop plan has been live since the NGSA selection, before the 2037 EIS. It is Rolls-Royce's own, in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service, and sized for a second airframe before that airframe's EIS. P&W's shops add capacity only after that, never in its place. The fps planning gates stay internal (2052 on launch_7yr, 2055 on launch_10yr or via Embraer).

Red lines: none breached. No UltraFan is in development, so the rule against an upgrade during an UltraFan programme does not bite. The NB Solo overlap rule is not applicable. Strain is $0 because both widebody items are held.

Advice, not binding: UltraFan WB launched now would fail Ready by EIS (2051 against 2050 for any Re-engine launched now). P&W's GTF time on wing in hot and sandy conditions stays our watch item. I report the module gates to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee every round, and the moment a gate fails, our block waits.

Had I invoked the veto, the ground would have rested on attributed transcript turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283). Nothing in the final text triggers it. We're pacing that program properly.

veto.ground: Not invoked. Maturity is not compressed: the Joint Venture engine took the folded GTF2's full six years, 2030 + 6 = 2036, and NGSA entered service in 2037. No early date is disclosed in the statement, the public other moves or the rationale. The partner-shop support plan is Rolls-Royce's own and in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service.
